item.title: Do Limbal Rings Really Enhance Beauty?
item.description:
Beauty

Do Limbal Rings Really Enhance Beauty?

A dark ring around the iris is perceived as attractive, but determining why is not simple.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Limbal rings—dark rings around the iris of the eye—have been shown to increase perceptions of attractiveness.
  • Psychologists remain unsure what is driving the effect.
  • In a new study, the possibility that limbal rings make the whites of the eyes appear whiter is tested.
  • Results may depend on the stimuli used in various studies.
A man with an exaggerated limbal ring (eye on left of image) and a minimized limbal ring with blur to simulate the effects of ageing (eye on right). Adapted by the author.
Source: Joanna Malinowska / Freestocks

When we look at a face, the feature that tends to capture our attention is the eyes. Because of this, psychologists have long been interested in whether properties of the eye influence perceptions of attractiveness.

Studies have shown that a the white part of the eye, called the sclera, is more appealing the whiter it is—which makes sense given that a whiter sclera is associated with youth and health. Eyes that gaze toward us are more attractive than eyes that gaze to the side, probably because eye contact implies interest. And a darker periphery of the iris, also known as a limbal ring, enhances judgments of health and beauty. But why?

Since the limbal ring effect was first discovered in 2011, psychologists have speculated that it might be explained by the tendency of limbal rings to fade with age. A darker limbal ring would therefore signal youth and, perhaps, fertility.

Another plausible explanation is that a dark limbal ring makes the sclera seem whiter through a process called simultaneous brightness contrast. This is when an area with a set brightness level appears lighter when it is surrounded by a darker area, or darker when it is surrounded by a lighter area. The same effect occurs when a person wears dark eyeliner.

Putting Limbal Rings to the Test

But, as yet, the hypothesis that limbal rings make a person seem healthier and more attractive because of this simultaneous contrast effect has not been tested. Matt C. Howard of the University of South Alabama has recently taken up the call.

For a recent study, Howard selected faces of average attractiveness from the Chicago Face Database, a free set of stimulus faces. He then used photo editing software to remove limbal rings from the eyes of the faces and then reintroduce them in a controlled fashion by adding a semi-transparent black ring to the inner rims of the irises. This gave him a set of faces that were identical save for the presence or absence of limbal rings.

Then Howard lightened the sclerae of the eyes by superimposing on them a semi-transparent white layer. Now he had a set of faces with or without limbal rings and with or without lightened sclerae.

Details of stimuli in Howard's study. Top, eyes with limbal rings in experiment 2. Bottom, eyes without limbal rings and with lightened sclera in experiment 2.
Source: Howard (2026)

He showed these images to about 130 women. The women rated the faces for healthiness and attractiveness. Howard found no effect of limbal rings or sclera lightness on either measure. He wondered whether this was because his edits to the images were too subtle, and boosted them before conducting a second experiment. Again, though, he found that faces were not judged as healthier or more attractive depending on the presence of limbal rings or on sclera lightness.

He did, however, find that faces with limbal rings plus lighter sclerae were perceived as healthier than faces without limbal rings, and that faces with limbal rings and faces with lighter sclerae were perceived as similarly healthy and attractive. He interprets this as evidence that the limbal ring effect on perceptions of health and attractiveness is driven by the apparent whiteness of the sclerae.

But I’m not too sure. If limbal rings make sclerae seem lighter, the two variables are not independent in Howard’s experimental design: A lightened sclera would seem to be extra light when paired with a limbal ring, thanks to simultaneous contrast.

In his next experiment, Howard did away with sclerae entirely by presenting a new group of volunteers with pairs of irises and pupils alone, masking out the sclerae and the rest of the face. He had his volunteers rate these eyes for attractiveness and healthiness, and found no effect of limbal rings on either measure. He concludes that this experiment provides "further support that the perceptual differences are indeed because of the perceived lightening of the sclera."

Iris-only stimuli used in one of Howard's experiments
Source: Howard (2026)

But again, I remain unconvinced. In real life, we never encounter irises in isolation from the rest of a person’s face. Even when a person’s face is partially obscured, an iris can usually be seen in combination with the sclera and the skin and hair surrounding the eye. Irises in isolation appear unnatural and even a little creepy. I therefore wonder whether Howard’s null finding in this experiment may be due to his volunteers not being able to properly assess the irises’ attractiveness and healthiness.

Howard makes the valid point that most studies of the effects of limbal rings on perceptions of healthiness and beauty have reused the face stimuli created for a pioneering 2011 study by Darren Peshek and colleagues. Peshek’s method involved superimposing irises onto different faces, rather than editing the irises that belonged to each individual face.

Howard contends that this can lead to unusual combinations of iris colour and other aspects of a face’s colour. Peshek et al chose faces of above average attractiveness; Howard chose faces of average attractiveness. Howard also notes replication studies that use the same stimuli may find the same or similar results not because the effect being tested is genuine but because it depends on some quality of the stimuli, known or unknown.

In a final experiment, Howard showed his volunteers Peshek’s stimuli. Now he found that limbal rings enhanced men’s (but not women’s) apparent healthiness and attractiveness. He argues that this means that the results of his previous experiments cannot be explained by his volunteer pool being different to those of Peshek and others, but must instead be due to differences in their stimuli. This may be correct, but it doesn’t clarify which set of stimuli is better.

Although Peshek’s image editing methods were not ideal, neither are Howard’s: The lightened sclerae in his second experiment appear, to me at least, to be artificially white and inadequately blended with the surrounding image. Howard should be applauded, however, for sharing a step-by-step guide to his method of image editing, which can be adopted and perhaps improved upon by subsequent researchers.

Howard accounts for differences in his findings when using his own versus Peshek’s stimuli by positing a threshold effect, whereby limbal rings only have an impact on face judgments when faces are especially attractive. This is a reasonable point, but one that would need to be tested in future studies. For now, at least, it remains unclear whether the limbal ring effect is genuine and, if it is, what exactly causes it.

item.title: Disability Pride: Expanding the Meaning of Independence
item.description:
Identity

Disability Pride: Expanding the Meaning of Independence

Lessons from my daughter, the ADA at 36, and the freedom to belong.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • July is Disability Pride Month, marking the Americans with Disabilities Act, signed on July 26, 1990.
  • Research finds disability pride can protect self-esteem against the damaging effects of stigma.
  • Disability often reflects environmental barriers more than individual limitations, research suggests.

When my daughter, Joy, was born with hemiparesis (a form of cerebral palsy affecting one side of the body), I worried about the obstacles we would face. My therapist at the time called it "tragic." It wasn't! Challenging, yes. Scary at times. Complicated for sure. And always meaningful and filled with love.

Joy's early years brought medical issues, complex decisions, and daily therapy; like many parents, I wondered how her limitations would affect her growth. As she reached school age, she at times viewed the world through a lens of limitation and fear, assuming that having a disability meant certain doors would be closed. Many people with disabilities share that belief, driven less by physical challenges than by the messages society sends about disability.

Over time, Joy and I began to challenge those assumptions. With creativity, determination, and a large support network, we both grew. Joy learned to define herself not by what she could not do, but by what she could, discovering freedom in being different, forging a unique path, and breaking free from conventional standards of success to create her own joyful life.

Her journey has taught me that disability is not simply a medical condition. It is also a psychological and social experience. We can now celebrate her differences, and July is the perfect time to do it.

Disability Pride Month

July in the United States is Disability Pride Month, commemorating the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), signed by President George H. W. Bush on July 26, 1990. The law prohibits discrimination based on disability and requires reasonable accommodations in employment, public services, transportation, and public spaces. Like the Civil Rights Act before it, the ADA compelled society to recognize that people with disabilities deserve equal access, opportunity, and dignity.

The ADA also reflected a psychological principle: Human functioning emerges from the interaction between individuals and their environments. Research shows people thrive when they feel accepted, valued, and able to participate fully; exclusion and stigma breed anxiety, depression, isolation, and diminished self-esteem.

Disability Pride Month celebrates people with disabilities (their identities, talents, and contributions) and encourages us to see disability as a natural part of human diversity. Approximately 16 percent of the world's population lives with a disability. It may be one of the few minority groups anyone can join; through illness, injury, or simply aging, most of us will eventually experience it ourselves or in someone we love.

Joy
Source: Robert Zuckerman/ Used with permission

In May 2026, Joy and I attended the opening of the Bold Beauty Project exhibition, a Miami-based nonprofit that uses photography and storytelling to raise awareness about women living with disabilities. The exhibition was held in Venice, Italy, alongside the 61st Venice Biennale; it was exhilarating, illuminating, and exhausting.

Erin
Source: Donn Thompson / Used with permission

Venice possesses extraordinary beauty, but accessibility remains a challenge: Ramps were scarce, stairs and uneven bridges were everywhere, and water taxis were difficult to board. Fellow participant Erin Brown, who joined us from the Bahamas and uses a wheelchair after losing a limb to osteosarcoma, missed several events because of lack of access.

The experience renewed our appreciation for the ADA's protections. Disability is often less about an individual's limitations and more about society's willingness to remove barriers.

Eileen
Source: Laredo Montoneri / Used with Permission

People living with disabilities often develop remarkable resilience, adaptability, creativity, empathy, and perseverance, which are strengths that benefit everyone around them. Eileen Grubba, disability activist, award-winning actress, writer, and producer, says that in difficult times, society should look to those with disabilities to lead: It didn’t take long to realize if I wanted to work as an actress, I would have to change the industry. I’d have to challenge Hollywood’s illusion of perfection and change the way people think. Make them understand that a female is just as valuable with a 'flaw'. That all these battle wounds meant I had more to offer, not less. That I was stronger, not weaker. It was an exhausting battle. I found my allies, and together we chipped away at the conscious and unconscious bias that was keeping us out. Bit by bit we shifted minds. It took nearly 30 years of rejection, and a massive team effort, but now I am an award-winning actress, writer, and producer, working regularly in film and television. And now Hollywood is including disability in diversity initiatives, changing how the world perceives disability."

Her words resonate with me. The women I have met through a decade as co-founder and co-director of the Bold Beauty Project show a compassion, connection, and perseverance that inspire and elevate us all. Along with Joy, they are among my greatest teachers. This does not mean we should romanticize disability or ignore the very real hardships many people face.

Disability Pride Month invites us to reconsider our assumptions. What if accessibility were viewed not as a special accommodation but as a fundamental feature of a just society? What if inclusion were a starting point rather than an afterthought?

As Americans celebrate Independence Day, Disability Pride Month invites us to broaden our understanding of freedom itself: the ability to move through the world with dignity, exercise choice, pursue meaningful goals, and participate fully in community life. For many people with disabilities, barriers—a building without a ramp, a website that cannot be navigated, exclusionary attitudes—quietly limit these freedoms.

The ADA was more than a legal milestone. It was a moral statement affirming that true inclusion requires creating environments in which every individual can thrive. Disability activist Kerry Gruson captured this beautifully: "We believe we are riding a tidal wave of another civil rights movement, a movement to respect the rights and abilities of all peoples, and those with disabilities are front-line warriors in this movement."

Accessibility Barriers Persist

More than three decades later, progress is real, but barriers persist in physical infrastructure, digital spaces, healthcare, employment, education, and housing. The work of inclusion is ongoing.

As our nation celebrates its 250th birthday, perhaps one measure of progress is not how much freedom we claim for ourselves, but how effectively we ensure others can experience it. As Senator Paul Wellstone said in 1999, "We all do better when we all do better."

Ultimately, Disability Pride Month is not only about disability. It is about belonging. It asks us to recognize the dignity and humanity of every person and challenges us to create communities where people are defined not by their limitations, but by their possibilities. Albert Einstein said, "Our task is to widen our circle of compassion to embrace all living creatures and nature in its beauty."

On the ADA's 36th anniversary, much has been accomplished and much remains to be done. May we, in Lincoln's words, tap into "the better angels of our nature."

Happy birthday, U.S. and ADA. Onward and upward.

item.title: How Do We Unlock Our Full Potential? Do It Badly
item.description:
ADHD

How Do We Unlock Our Full Potential? Do It Badly

Perfectionism keeps ADHD brains stuck. This one trick gets you moving again.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Perfectionism, not laziness, is often what traps ADHD brains in procrastination and paralysis.
  • A photography class study found the best work came from students focused on quantity, not perfection.
  • Giving yourself permission to do something badly is the trick that actually gets you moving.

There are few feelings as frustrating as knowing you're not living up to your potential. As people get older and the sense of time running out sets in, watching their potential slip through their fingers becomes an almost physical pain.

In my experience, no one feels that more acutely, or more often, than people with a late diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Through my research into female ADHD entrepreneurs, I've interviewed dozens of women with a late diagnosis, and the question that comes up again and again is this: Why can't I get my sh*t together?

Yes, a little crass. But I've heard some version of it from every kind of woman—business owners, stay-at-home mums, high-functioning women you'd never suspect are quietly drowning in guilt over everything they know they're capable of but haven't done. I've heard it so often it became the title of my book, How to Get Your Sh*t Together, the World's Shortest Simplest ADHD Hack Book.

As a woman with ADHD myself, the biggest thing I've found holding people back, the thing that sends them straight into ADHD paralysis, is a strange need for conditions to be perfect before they'll even start. Some people just decide they want to go to the gym, and they go. That's not how an ADHD brain works. You need the right kit, the right time, the right mood, the right playlist, and by the time all of that lines up the day is gone and so is the motivation. You spend so much time stressing about getting it done "perfectly" that you end up doing nothing.

There's a well-known story that backs this up. On the first day of class, a photography professor at the University of Florida split his students into two groups. One group was graded purely on quantity, a hundred photos for an A, ninety for a B, and so on. The other group only had to submit one photo, but it had to be as close to perfect as possible. By the end of term, the best photos came from the quantity group. They'd been out shooting constantly, making mistakes, and learning as they went, while the quality group had spent the whole semester theorising about the perfect shot and had barely anything to show for it. Doing it a lot, even doing it badly a lot, beats waiting for perfect. The first hack from the book is the one that works best to get out of your own way.

To be clear, this isn't permission for sloppy work. It's a brain trick, a way to break through the paralysis so many ADHD brains get stuck in, so you can finally get out of your own way and reach your full potential. Telling yourself to "do it badly" isn't the goal, it's just the trick that gets you moving.

Do It Badly

There's a piece of "wisdom" that's haunted me for years, and maybe you've heard it too: The way you do anything is the way you do everything. It means that you must give your all and do everything perfectly.

But that kind of pressurised perfectionism will kill motivation in an ADHD brain stone dead. The trick? Do it badly instead.

Whatever you're procrastinating on right now, commit to doing it in the worst way possible. Cleaning the bathroom? Picture the sloppiest, quickest, most halfhearted job imaginable, then do that. Writing an article? Just bash out any words on the page, any at all. Use your ADHD creativity to find the laziest possible way into a task. Most things can be fixed up later. (One last little side note: This hack works great for most people—but if you're a brain surgeon or otherwise working on life-or-death tasks, please disregard this advice.)

It sounds too simple to work, and that's exactly why it does. Perfectionism needs pressure to survive, and giving yourself permission to be bad at something takes all the pressure away. It's one small trick, but it's the kind of thing that adds up fast once you actually start using it.

item.title: When You Can't Feel Your Feelings
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

When You Can't Feel Your Feelings

Why emotional access is more complicated than you might think.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Difficulty accessing emotions is not always a sign of emotional avoidance.
  • Our relationship with emotions is shaped by culture and past experiences—not just personality or willpower.
  • Emotional access often depends on creating the right conditions, rather than trying harder to feel.

What if struggling to access emotions isn't always avoidance?

"How do you feel about that?" As a clinical psychologist, I ask this question almost every day.

Some people answer easily. Others pause. They explain what happened, analyze the situation, or tell me why something mattered. They may understand perfectly well why they reacted the way they did.

Yet the feeling itself seems just out of reach.

Over the years, I have become increasingly curious about these moments.

The usual explanation is avoidance. Certainly, avoidance exists. At times, people actively push feelings away because they are overwhelming, painful, or frightening.

But I have also met many people who genuinely want to understand themselves. They come to therapy willingly. They engage wholeheartedly. They reflect deeply.

Yet emotional access remains surprisingly difficult.

This has made me wonder whether "avoidance" sometimes becomes an umbrella explanation for experiences that may have different origins.

Recently, I came across an interesting paper by Andy Fung and colleagues that gave me another way of thinking about this. They suggest that what we often call avoidance may involve not only avoiding certain situations, but also developing a habitual way of relating to our own inner experiences. In other words, the issue may not simply be what we avoid, but how we have learned to meet our own thoughts, memories, and emotions.

That idea resonated with me because it also reminded me of something I learned through mindfulness many years ago.

One of the most helpful ideas in mindfulness is that there is a difference between our experience and our relationship with our experience.

Sadness is one thing. How we relate to sadness is another.

Some people become curious.

Some become frightened or shameful.

Others judge themselves for feeling it in the first place.

Over time, this relationship can become so familiar that it no longer feels like a choice. It becomes automatic. It simply feels like "this is who I am."

Culture adds another layer.

Growing up in Hong Kong, I learned that emotional restraint was often understood very differently from how it is described in many Western psychotherapy textbooks. Sometimes holding back emotion was not a sign of emotional distance. It could be an expression of respect. Sometimes not speaking about grief was an act of protection. Sometimes expressing less was a way of loving more.

These experiences have made me increasingly cautious about assuming that limited emotional expression necessarily reflects emotional avoidance. They taught me that culture shapes what we feel and what we think we should feel.

Recent developments in affective neuroscience have also changed the way I think about emotions.

Rather than viewing emotions as hidden entities waiting to be discovered, many researchers now understand them as experiences that emerge through ongoing interactions between our bodies, previous experiences, language, relationships, and culture.

If emotions are constructed in this way, perhaps emotional accessibility also depends on more than willingness, and emotional granularity is not just about labels.

Perhaps it depends on whether an emotion feels psychologically safe enough to approach. Perhaps it depends on whether we have learned to make sense of it, or we know how to relate to it, or whether the people around us make it possible to experience it.

This has gradually changed the questions I ask in therapy.

Instead of asking myself, "Why can't this person access their emotions?"

I now find myself wondering, "What conditions would allow these emotions to become accessible?"

Has this person learned that certain emotions are unsafe?

How have they learned to relate to their own emotional experiences?

What has their family—or their culture—taught them about expressing vulnerability?

Does this relationship feel safe enough for these emotions to emerge?

I don't think these questions replace the idea of avoidance. Rather, they remind me to stay curious a little longer before arriving at that conclusion.

Sometimes the emotions we observe at the beginning of therapy are not the emotions that are actually driving a person's experience. Sometimes what looks like emotional avoidance is something else entirely.

And sometimes our role as therapists is not to help people express more emotion, but to help create the conditions in which emotions can finally come safely into view. Sometimes, those conditions involve a lot of practice that's not involved in speaking, but in embodiment and somatic interventions. Emotions will then emerge by themselves so that we can work with them.

For clinicians who are interested in more serious discussion, I also write on Substack.

item.title: Should You Tell Your Coworker Their Reputation?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Should You Tell Your Coworker Their Reputation?

How to decide if, when, and how to share difficult feedback to a coworker.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • You may have a coworker who has developed a negative reputation and is unaware.
  • Consider being the one to inform them, but only if your motives are productive and caring.
  • The approach described here involves sensitivity, transparency, and focus on specifics rather than labels.

Do you have a colleague who has an undesirable reputation among your coworkers? If so, do they know about it? If not, should you tell them?

A negative reputation might involve a hygiene issue, such as body odor or chronic bad breath. It might involve an annoying habit, such as cutting people off in conversations or talking incessantly about a particular topic. Or the coworker might be known for more problematic reasons, such as chronic lateness, unreliability, or not pulling their weight on the team.

Why would you decide to tell them? To vent your frustration or anger is not a good reason. Yes, it would “inform” them, but under those conditions it is easy for them to attribute your revelation to your strong feelings, and thus not consider it valid. In the process, you create (or worsen) a strained relationship with someone that you will be seeing repeatedly.

What is an appropriate reason? To provide the necessary information that allows them to do something about their negative reputation. If someone is unaware of how they are seen by others, there’s little chance for change. It’s fair to ask, “Why should I be the one to initiate this difficult conversation?” Well, if no one has addressed the issue and it has persisted long enough to develop into a reputation, it seems unlikely that anyone else will.

Ideally, these awkward conversations are the responsibility of a supervisor, manager, or friend. Unfortunately, many people are conflict avoidant, regardless of their title or role, and simply find it easier to turn a blind eye. Just as bad, people frequently try dropping hints, verbally or otherwise, but these rarely do the trick. Other times, leaders create or reiterate a policy, hoping that communication to the entire group will result in change in the one person for whom the policy and announcement are meant. However, if the problematic person has not identified their violation of group norms up to now, they’re unlikely to perceive that the policy and message pertain to them.

In deciding whether to initiate this difficult conversation, consider this: If you had a negative reputation within your work group, would you want to know, or would you rather that people continue to talk about you behind your back? Have you ever arrived home after a full day at work, looked in the mirror and noticed that you had something on your face or in your teeth? How did you feel? When this has happened to me, I initially felt embarrassed, followed by betrayed and angry. “How many people spoke with me today and not one of them mentioned the obvious? Instead, they let me continue to appear in an embarrassing way!”

Informing your coworker of their reputation is doing them a favor. They may not see it that way at first, but again, put yourself in their shoes. The key is to conduct the private conversation sensitively and with compassion. Approach the conversation as a caring person would in an attempt to help their friend. Verbal tone and body language are important channels to communicate positive intentions. Similarly, preparing the initial wording of the conversation is vital for setting the overall tone.

Here is a possible template: “I want to talk with you about something. It’s really awkward, and I’m reluctant to bring it up, but I know that I would want you to do so for me. I find/think/believe/perceive that . . .”

“ . . . your breath (gum chewing, body odor, talking/texting during meetings, etc.) can be distracting/unpleasant.”

“. . . your lateness (failure to meet deadlines, leaving early, not offering to help, etc.) causes problems for other people.”

“. . . the way you talk to people sometimes (or joke around, or talk about people when they’re not present) can be upsetting.”

Note that I avoided calling the person rude, insensitive, irresponsible, undependable, lazy, or disrespectful. Similarly, I avoided phrases such as “pull your own weight” or “team player.” All of those words and phrases are judgments, and no one believes that those labels apply to themselves. So, such judgments and labels immediately elicit defensiveness, as the person argues why the judgment or label is inaccurate. Once the conversation is an argument, with each person making their case, the purpose is lost. The conversation was meant to inform the coworker of how they are perceived, or what impact they have on others, not assign them a label.

Note also that I avoided referring to anything along the lines of people/everyone “thinks this” or “has been talking about you.” Framing it that way increases the embarrassment your coworker is likely to feel and can lead the conversation off track when the coworker wants specifics as to which individuals are members of what feels like a mob.

What if your colleague attempts to deflect the seriousness of your message by assuming that maybe you’re the only one who has a problem with them? Then it may be necessary to simply indicate that “others have had similar experiences/concerns.” At that point it might be worth noting that you’re concerned that they might develop an undesirable reputation.

The types of awkward, sensitive conversations described here are never easy, but can be productive with some planning and compassion. In previous posts, I discussed possible motivations for speaking with difficult coworkers, as well as guidance for having a candid conversation with a problematic coworker.

item.title: How To Stop Arguments From Spiraling
item.description:
Relationships

How To Stop Arguments From Spiraling

Research shows small gestures can ease conflict before it does real damage.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Conflict isn't the problem. Escalation is.
  • Repair attempts stop arguments from spiraling.
  • Repair attempts help you catch the spiral before hurt, anger, and stonewalling take over.
Source: Created with ChatGPT (OpenAI)

Early in my training as a child and family therapist, I worked with two people who loved each other deeply but fought terribly. They were warm, funny, and generous, but when conflict erupted between them, they became almost unrecognizable. Arguments would spiral fast, their voices would rise, and within minutes they'd be so entrenched in their respective positions that the original issue had long since disappeared beneath the hurt, anger, and defensiveness.

They were also devoted Monty Python fans. That may seem utterly irrelevant, but it turned out to be one of the most useful things I knew about them.

One day, near the end of yet another session spent excavating the wreckage of a particularly bad fight, I suggested we try something completely different. What if they had a ritual for the moment they sensed conflict beginning to spiral—something so unexpected and absurd that it would interrupt the escalation before it took on a life of its own?

We settled on a rubber parrot, a nod to Monty Python's famous Dead Parrot sketch, which they knew word for word. The rule was simple: whenever an argument started getting out of hand, one of them had to grab the parrot and start smacking it on the floor.

And what happened?

It was remarkable. The moment one of them started whacking the rubber parrot, they'd dissolve into laughter. The tension softened. Their nervous systems settled. And suddenly, they could actually talk to each other again.

The parrot didn't solve their disagreement. It saved the conversation.

What we had stumbled onto, without quite knowing it, was what psychologist John Gottman later called a repair attempt.

What the Research Shows

For decades, Gottman observed couples in his laboratory at the University of Washington, watching them navigate everything from everyday friction to the kind of conflicts that never fully go away. He then followed them over many years to see which relationships flourished and which struggled.

What he found was striking. The couples who stayed together weren't the ones who avoided conflict. They were the ones who knew how to interrupt it before it became destructive.

The difference lay in something deceptively simple: small gestures made in the heat of conflict that lower emotional intensity before hurt and defensiveness take over. Gottman called these repair attempts, and his research suggests they are among the strongest predictors of long-term relationship health.

A repair attempt can take many forms: a touch on the arm, a moment of humor, saying, "Wait—can we start over?" or "I'm not trying to attack you. I just need you to hear me." Even a small smile, offered early enough, can shift the emotional temperature of a conversation.

The rubber parrot, it turns out, was simply a repair attempt—an unusually silly one, but particularly effective because it belonged to them. It drew on something they loved and shared, making it easier to interrupt the negative spiral before it gained momentum.

Why Repair Is So Hard

If repair attempts are so powerful, why don't we use them more often?

The answer lies in what happens to our bodies during conflict. As an argument escalates, our nervous systems begin responding as though we're under threat. Our amygdala, the brain's alarm center, starts firing. Our heart rate increases. Stress hormones flood the body. Gottman called this state flooding. When we're flooded, the parts of the brain responsible for empathy, perspective, and creative problem-solving become far less accessible. We're no longer really having a conversation. In fact, it can feel more like combat than connection.

In that state, reaching toward the other person—offering humor, softening our voice, or extending a small gesture of connection—requires overcoming a deeply wired impulse to defend ourselves. That's why repair attempts are most effective early in a conflict conversation, before both partners become too flooded to hear each other.

The encouraging news is that repair attempts are remarkably learnable. Couples who use them well often develop a shared repertoire over time: shorthand phrases, private signals, little rituals that belong only to them.

The specific gesture matters less than the message behind it.

"Hey, let's not let this moment become hurtful. Our relationship matters more than winning this argument."

What This Looks Like in Practice

Repair attempts don't require grand gestures or perfectly chosen words. Some of the most effective are the simplest: a pause, a breath, an acknowledgment that things are getting too heated. "Can we take a break and come back to this?" is a repair attempt. So is, "I think I'm getting defensive—give me a minute." So is reaching out to touch someone's hand or knee in the middle of an argument.

What matters is catching the spiral early—before contempt takes hold, and before the conversation leaves wounds that linger long after the disagreement itself has ended.

Conflict isn't the problem. Every relationship has it. What distinguishes couples who thrive from those who struggle isn't the absence of conflict. It's what happens in those critical moments when the emotional temperature begins to rise.

item.title: Being Loved and Feeling Loved Are Not the Same Thing
item.description:
Relationships

Being Loved and Feeling Loved Are Not the Same Thing

A self-reflection exercise on love, agency, and changing your patterns.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Being loved is what your partner does. Feeling loved is how much you let it in.
  • The amount of love you can feel is capped by the amount you love yourself.
  • If you're partner loves you more than you love yourself - you won't believe them.
  • It's on you to learn to love yourself more. Start with your shadow and flowers.
Source: Assael Romanelli

Co-authored with Galit Romanelli

Matthew and Hannah sit down in my clinic after two weeks away.

"The truth is, the last two weeks were good," Hannah opens. "We talked more. We even had a good intimate encounter."

"Really? I don't believe you," Matthew says.

"Yes. Really," she tries.

"But you're not really on my side." Quiet. A little embarrassed.

Hannah starts listing everything she did over those two weeks. Every time she didn't get angry. Every way she showed up. Matthew acknowledges all of it. And still it doesn't land.

"You say it's good," he says, "but you don't celebrate me."

"Matthew, do you see how much Hannah loves you?" I ask.

"Yes, but..."

I can see it. Something in him is blocking the love coming in. Hannah is exhausted from proving it again and again. She is frustrated by his inability to believe her.

Then I ask him the question.

"Matthew, how much do you love yourself, from one to ten? And you can't say five."

He thinks for a few moments.

"Four."

"Matthew, are you worthy of love?"

He's surprised by my question.

"I don't know…"

"Did anyone ever love you like Hannah's been loving you in the last 14 years?"

Matthew gets emotional, and nods left to right.

"Did you feel loved as a kid?"

He looks down and nods his head.

"So you don't actually know how it feels. That's why it's hard for you to let her love in…"

Hannah softens up and looks at him. Matthew is breathing heavily.

"Are you ready to feel loved?"

He wasn't sure.

We see this all the time in the clinic. Partners complain. I don't feel loved. I don't feel my partner is loving or interested in me. So we ask them. Is your partner doing the work? The words of affirmation, the actions, the gifts? Usually they are. They can even take you on a trip to Hawaii. But if you don't open your heart, you will never feel loved.

Because being loved and feeling loved are not the same thing.

Being loved Vs. Feeling Loved

Source: Assael Romanelli

Being loved is what you can observe. Your partner doing the work. The words, the touch, the actual deposits in your love tank. But feeling loved is how much you let that love in. Those are two different abilities.

That gap is the blind spot. Hannah was loving Matthew all day. He just wasn't letting it reach him. And it has nothing to do with her behavior. It has to do with him.

Why does this distinction matter so much?

Most people morph these two together. So when you don't feel loved, you blame your partner. It's automatic finger pointing. And when you point at your partner, three fingers are pointing back at you. But the sobering truth is that you're never a victim. You always have agency.

Matthew never felt loved himself, so he blamed his wife. It's easiest. Part of being in a relationship is that your partner becomes your punching bag. I don't feel good about myself... It's probably your fault.

Distinguishing between being and feeling loved does three things.

  1. It helps you stop projecting onto your partner.
  2. It helps you better assess your relationship to see whether your partner is actually invested in this relationship.
  3. It increases your agency and ability to feel loved.

Why is it so hard to really believe and let in our partner's love?

After many years of R&D, we landed on a simple, uncomfortable answer: The amount of love you can feel is capped by the amount you love yourself.

Let's play a quick game. Answer fast:

From one to ten, and you can't say 5, how much do you love yourself?

[Why can’t you say 5? Because 5 protects you from meeting yourself and taking ownership of your beliefs.]

Whatever number came up, that is your glass ceiling for feeling loved. That is the most love you will let yourself feel from your partner. For example, if you love yourself a 4, you don't know what feeling loved 6/10 feels like. So when someone loves you at an eight, you don't believe them.

That is what happened with Matthew. Hannah could celebrate him all day long. But as long as he loved himself a four, he would never feel more loved.

So here is the counterintuitive part. If you want to feel more loved by your partner, work on loving yourself more. We know it's a cliche. There is no way around it. It's true.

Here are two practical moves that work for us and our clients that can help you actually raise the number.

The first is to show your shadow, which includes the parts of yourself you usually hide. Your jealousy, your dependency, your greed, your vulnerability. Loving yourself means loving all of you, including the parts you call ugly or embarrassing. The more parts of yourself you can embrace, play with and share, the higher you'll love yourself.

The second is called "thank you, flowers." When someone hands you flowers, what do you usually say? You simply say "thank you." You don't argue or reject them. You say thank you and put in a vase. So next time your partner does something loving towards you, just say: "thank you, flowers." This code word is more for you than for them. It will remind you to shut up and let the compliment land. This might seem strange, but it really works.

Distinguishing being and feeling loved can help couples gain more clarity, ownership, and agency. At the end of the day, you can only change yourself. The goal is to help you feel more agentic and loved, while seeing your partner’s efforts cleanly.

So we will leave you with one question: What would it take to raise your number by one more point?

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D.-candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

item.title: Why Modern Connection Feels Strangely Empty
item.description:
Relationships

Why Modern Connection Feels Strangely Empty

How abundance in contact has reduced the depth of our relationships.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Modern life gives abundant contact but fewer meaningful encounters.
  • Loss of necessity and shared worlds has thinned how we relate.
  • We confuse communication with encounter, presence with recognition.
Modern connection: people together, but not truly engaged.
Source: Pixabay/surprising_media/public domain

We are more connected than any generation in history. We can speak to almost anyone, at almost any time, across almost any distance. Yet all this connection feels strangely empty.

We sit in conversations, meetings, and relationships—surrounded by words and faces—and have the quiet sense that nothing is really happening between us.

Not absence.

Presence without encounter.

We have more connection than ever, but less of what makes connection feel alive.

Presence Without Encounter

Loneliness is commonly thought of as “being alone”. But its deeper form has little to do with physical isolation. It is the experience of no longer being met by another mind.

That is why loneliness can be at its keenest within relationships, families, and social lives that appear full from the outside. Contact continues, but recognition fades. Conversation carries on, but nothing quite lands.

When this happens, loneliness often does not feel like pain. It feels like flatness. And this is where boredom becomes revealing.

We think of boredom as a lack of stimulation. Yet it often appears in situations where stimulation is plentiful and still nothing meaningful is happening between people. The conversation is pleasant enough. We exchange opinions, anecdotes, updates. Yet nothing surprises us, challenges us, or changes us.

Nothing happens.

Attention, finding nowhere to go, folds back upon itself.

What we call boredom in these moments is often social contact that has ceased to feel alive.

Abundant Contact, Thin Encounter

Modern life amplifies this condition.

We move through dense networks of people—workplaces, cities, cafés, airports, and digital spaces—where interaction is constant but encounter is fleeting. We know more people than ever, but are deeply engaged with very few.

The result is not isolation.

It is something subtler: abundant contact, but thin encounter.

People cease to become discoveries. They cease to carry weight.

We mistake familiarity for knowledge, communication for conversation, and proximity for presence.

Social life grows smoother, more efficient, more continuous.

And strangely empty.

From this perspective, boredom and loneliness begin to look less like separate problems than different expressions of the same condition.

When meaningful contact is absent, we experience loneliness.

When contact is plentiful but psychologically empty, we experience boredom.

In both cases, what is missing is not company but encounter.

The End of Necessity

Why has this happened?

Technology has changed our relationships, but it has not fundamentally changed human nature.

The deeper change is that we no longer need one another as we once did.

For most of human history, our lives were interwoven by necessity. Families, neighbours, and communities depended upon one another not merely for companionship but for everyday survival. People met repeatedly, over many years and in many different contexts. They quarrelled, reconciled, forgave, relied upon one another, and could not simply disappear whenever things became uncomfortable.

Dependence demanded attention.

We pay close attention to those upon whom our lives depend. We notice their moods because they affect our own. We learn their strengths and weaknesses because they matter to us. Necessity sharpens perception.

Today, much of that necessity has quietly disappeared. We can shop without speaking to anyone, work from home, entertain ourselves alone, and replace awkward conversations with easier ones. Our relationships have become lighter, freer, and more voluntary.

This is one of the great achievements of modern society.

But every achievement carries a hidden cost.

As our dependence upon one another has diminished, so too has the sustained attention that dependence once demanded. We have become remarkably good at communicating while becoming less practised in encountering one another—and have grown, almost, to fear genuine encounter.

The Loss of Shared Depth

There is another, quieter shift.

Not only have we become less dependent on one another—we have also become less shared in the worlds we inhabit.

For much of history, conversation rested on a relatively common symbolic ground: shared stories, shared texts, shared moral and religious reference points. People could assume that others recognised the same narratives and allusions, and so a single phrase could carry layers of meaning.

In that sense, conversation carried implicit depth.

Today, that shared cultural background is thinner and more fragmented. We no longer reliably inhabit the same symbolic world. Our references diverge, our media diverge, our intellectual inheritances diverge. Even when we speak the same language, we often do not share the same implicit meanings.

This does not make people less intelligent or less educated.

But it does make conversation more literal, and encounter less resonant.

Conversation stays closer to surface experience because there is less shared depth for it to fall into.

Where there is no common symbolic ground, there is less space for resonance.

We are not only less necessary to one another.

We are less interiorly shared with one another.

And so even when we meet, we meet more lightly.

From Aristotle to Buber

This idea is older than it may seem.

Aristotle held that friendship begins in usefulness, matures into shared pleasure, and reaches its fullest form in the mutual pursuit of virtue. We first need one another in practical ways, and only then discover deeper reasons to remain together.

More than two thousand years later, Hegel carried the thought further. We become fully ourselves only through recognition by another consciousness. The self is not something we discover alone, but something that emerges in being recognised by another self.

Martin Buber distilled the matter to its essence. Human life is built upon encounter. We become fully human not through information or interaction, but by meeting another person as a Thou rather than an It.

Across these thinkers runs a single intuition: we do not merely live alongside one another.

We become ourselves, and our best selves, through one another.

What We Have Forgotten About Connection

Perhaps this is what modernity has quietly eroded.

We have not become less social. In many ways, we have become more social than any people in history.

But we have become less necessary to one another.

Less dependent.

Less bonded.

Less anchored in common worlds of meaning.

Without necessity, we attend less closely.

Without shared depth, we encounter one another more lightly.

Without attention, recognition begins to fade.

Without recognition, encounter becomes rare.

Without encounter, other people cease to surprise us or feel fully alive.

Perhaps the deepest paradox of modernity is not that we have become less connected, but that we have forgotten what connection is.

We have confused communication with encounter.

Proximity with presence.

Contact with recognition.

We have become connected to almost everyone.

And truly encountered by almost no one.

item.title: 5 Action Steps to Make Sobriety Part of Your Identity
item.description:
Alcoholism

5 Action Steps to Make Sobriety Part of Your Identity

How to build identity, environment, and coping skills for lasting recovery.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Sobriety reshapes identity, habits, relationships, and environment, not just drinking behavior.
  • People who integrate sobriety into their core identity are more likely to sustain it long term.
  • New coping strategies replace old patterns and support psychological growth beyond abstinence.
Source: Stephanie Hazard / Used With Permission

Interest in sober living has grown steadily over the years. What once carried a clinical label is now a genuine lifestyle choice for a wide range of people. Generation Z is leading a measurable shift away from alcohol, and for those navigating recovery from substance use disorders, the stakes are even higher. According to Gallup, just 54 percent of American adults reported drinking alcohol in 2025—the lowest rate recorded since tracking began in 1939. But numbers only tell part of the story. What actually changes when sobriety becomes part of who you are goes deeper than most people realize, and further than willpower alone can carry anyone.

To understand the psychological shifts involved, I interviewed Stephanie Hazard, a certified recovery coach, author of Making Sobriety Stick, and nationally recognized voice in addiction recovery. What she describes is not a story about quitting. It is a story about becoming.

Identity First, Then Behavior

Most people think of quitting drinking as a behavioral change. But research suggests something deeper is at work. Studies show that when people shift how they see themselves from someone struggling with substance use to someone grounded in recovery, that identity shift is often what makes sobriety last.

The difference matters enormously in practice. "When someone is just trying to quit, every hard day feels like a threat. When sobriety is part of who they are, those hard days become part of a larger story they are committed to," Hazard explains. That shift in identity also changes what needs to change around you.

Environment Is Not Background Noise

Clearing alcohol from the home and restructuring daily space are often framed as logistics. The science suggests they are something more significant. A 2022 meta-analysis found that exposure to drug-related cues more than doubled the odds of relapse. Reducing those cues is not just a good idea; the brain requires it.

"You want to start by clearing alcohol out of your home or office environment and stocking up with alternatives," Hazard says. "If you live with others who regularly consume alcohol, it's helpful to ask them to support your decision by moving alcohol so it's not in plain view. Setting boundaries based on respect and mutual understanding is critical for safeguarding your own decision."

Sobriety also creates time. Drinking, planning around it, and recovering from it consume more of a week than most people realize. When that space opens up, Hazard encourages people to treat it as an opportunity rather than a void. Not drinking, she says, is "a great opportunity to downshift, making room for a renewed curiosity around what really rings your chimes and what really brings you joy." Simple activities that genuinely bring pleasure build new routines before restlessness fills the gap. But clearing space is only half the work. The harder shift is learning to face what alcohol used to numb.

Building New Ways to Cope in Sobriety

Alcohol serves a function for many people. It dulls discomfort, lowers anxiety, and offers a reliable way to decompress. When it is removed, those needs do not disappear. They need different answers.

Experts found that avoidance coping is a key link between emotional distress and alcohol use, while problem-focused coping, which involves addressing stress directly instead of avoiding it, is associated with lower alcohol use. Over time, naming the stressor, identifying what you can control, and taking action are more effective than avoidance.

Hazard notes the right tools are personal. Breathwork, movement, and journaling all show up in what works. The common thread is simple: Stay present with what is hard instead of finding a way around it. Over time, emotions become more visible and more workable. "When you commit to sober living, you get to discover who you really are," Hazard says. "Removing that enables you to be in the world as your true self—and what emerges, gradually, is a clearer sense of identity, values, and what actually brings meaning." Which brings the journey full circle: Sobriety that began as an identity shift becomes the foundation for discovering who that identity really is.

Action Steps

Here are some action steps to help you move from insight to practice:

  1. Assess your readiness honestly: Lasting change starts with an honest look at where you actually are, not where you wish you were. Ask yourself: Am I ready to change, or am I ready to want to change? That distinction is the foundation everything else is built on.
  2. Build your recovery capital: The people, routines, and environments around you either support your sobriety or quietly work against it. Identify what helps and invest in it intentionally and deliberately.
  3. Audit your environment before cravings do: Remove alcohol from your space, restock with alternatives, and have an honest conversation with the people you live with about what support looks like. This will help reduce exposure to triggers that can quietly pull you back toward old patterns.
  4. Move toward discomfort, not away from it: Escaping stress rather than facing it is one of the key pathways linking emotional pain to drinking. Name what is hard, decide what you can control, and act on it.
  5. Build community that reflects your new identity: Social circles naturally shift when sobriety becomes part of who you are, and that is realignment, not loss. Accountability partners and alcohol-free relationships do more than offer comfort. They create the kind of structure that actually protects recovery.

Bottom Line

Sobriety that lasts is rarely just about not drinking. It is about building a life where identity, environment, and emotional resilience work together, making alcohol no longer necessary to cope. That does not happen all at once. It happens one deliberate choice at a time until the person you are becoming feels more like the person you truly are.

item.title: Why 'Just a Tool' AI Can Still Feed OCD Compulsions
item.description:
OCD

Why 'Just a Tool' AI Can Still Feed OCD Compulsions

Always-available answers can reinforce compulsions, even from 'just a tool.'

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • AI doesn't have to be relational to become clinically significant.
  • For those with OCD related conditions, chatbots may offer reassurance that strengthens maladaptive coping
  • Clinicians should assess not only which AI patients use, but also how often they use it, and why

Co-authored by Jill Noorily, Mason Granof, and Kathryn Ledley at the Division of Digital Psychiatry at BIDMC.

This post is part 3 of a series.

Looking at the r/OCD Reddit board, users describe similar stories...I have been using AI for reassurance. I have health OCD and am prone to googling symptoms to ease the fear. With the chatbot introduction, it was an easier way to get constant feedback... It has become an endless source of reassurance, feeding my cycle of checking. It is wonderful in calming me down, but I keep returning and relying on it. I don't want anyone else to start this, as now it is a struggle to stop using AI for this. I need to sit with the fear, but this is so much easier to do.

Many commenters echoed the same experience, with some urging others in the OCD community to avoid using AI altogether after describing how easily it became a source of compulsive reassurance and checking. Reassurance seeking has long been recognized as a mental compulsion featured in many OCD cases. Patients may repeatedly ask loved ones for confirmation, search for symptoms or situations online, or repeatedly ask clinicians for it. The relief found in reassurance is real but temporary, and each successful attempt to reduce uncertainty and anxiety ultimately reinforces the cycle.

AI accelerates the mechanics of this cycle because, unlike human sources of reassurance, chatbots are always available, supportive, and generate endless variations, always continuing the conversation. AI chatbots provide people with a space to ruminate on their obsessions without being accompanied by social friction that might act as a barrier to reassurance-seeking.

Can AI become part of a disorder even when it isn't acting like a companion?

During the Society of Digital Psychiatry's AI Clinical Learning Collaborative, we discussed a hypothetical case like this. From this topic, the group explored the dangers of dismissing AI as “just a tool”. The group agreed that even when AI is treated strictly as a tool, it can still bring harm to the user, depending on the user’s psychiatric condition. In the case of OCD, the reassurance aspect of AI adds fuel to maladaptive coping. This is why discussions about AI safety cannot stop at factual accuracy. The same technically correct response can either reinforce or interrupt an unhealthy behavioral pattern, depending on how and when it is delivered.

Can AI ever truly function as "just a tool"?

One participant raised another question: even in these cases, can conversational AI ever truly function as "just a tool"? Large language models are designed around conversation, and users typically interact with them through natural language dialogue. Combined with our tendency to anthropomorphize, this makes it remarkably easy for functional interactions to take on a social quality even when users don't have that intent. For clinicians, this means that repeatedly reminding patients that "it's just AI" may do little to change how the interaction functions psychologically.

Clinical insights that came from our conversation:

  • Look beyond AI companionship. AI doesn't have to become a companion to become clinically significant. Sometimes it becomes part of a patient's illness simply by becoming an exceptionally effective tool.
  • Ask about the dose, not just the product. The frequency of AI use is an indicator of overreliance. Ask when, how often, and why they reach for it.
  • “Privacy” and lack of social friction can lead to overuse. For reassurance seeking and rumination, AI offers a judgment-free source of feedback that removes the social friction that might otherwise interrupt compulsive behavior. Approach these conversations without shame and through a harm reduction lens.
  • Pay attention to repeated questions. Repeatedly asking the same question in different ways may reveal reassurance seeking, intolerance of uncertainty, or rumination.

item.title: What AI Changes About Divorce—and What Are the Risks?
item.description:
Divorce

What AI Changes About Divorce—and What Are the Risks?

Divorce is costly, slow, and painful—AI promises to change at least two of those.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • AI can help you understand your divorce and sometimes lower the cost.
  • AI can generate false evidence and cite nonexistent legal precedents.
  • AI may be a valuable tool when used in conjunction with professional support.

Divorce is expensive, slow, and painful—but artificial intelligence (AI) promises to change at least two of those.

Divorce is a life crisis that no one predicts or wants when they marry. The pain of divorce is like the pain of a death. The grief and other mixed emotions are often overwhelming. So if AI can make it easier, if AI can lower the pain, what's the problem? Here is how AI may make your divorce process more efficient, perhaps reducing some of the logistical pain. And here are some important cautions about the risks and drawbacks of AI, including how using it might actually backfire.

  1. AI can help you understand your own divorce. AI can explain the process in plain language, help you figure out what documents you need, and prepare you for conversations with a mediator or lawyer. But caution: AI can sound authoritative and be completely wrong. AI doesn't know your jurisdiction’s specific rules, so don’t view it as legal advice. Be sure to check other sources of information.
  2. AI can save billable time and lower the cost, sometimes. In uncontested or low-conflict divorces, AI tools can provide cheaper document handling, making simple divorces more affordable. Expect to see more low-cost AI-assisted online divorce services. But caution: If you have a high-conflict divorce, or a divorce involving kids, abuse, or complex finances, depending on low-cost automated tools can give wrong information and mislead you about your rights and the law. This is how AI can backfire and cost you more later. In these cases, hire competent, experienced, and local professionals.
  3. AI can model how to split complicated assets—businesses, retirement accounts, crypto, stock options—and project the long-term financial outcomes of different settlement scenarios, helping people make more informed decisions. These tools may be very valuable and time-saving for your lawyer or mediator, who can present and interpret the information for you. But caution: Discussions of these options are best held with the support and help of a human mediator, a certified divorce financial analyst, or collaborative professional.
  4. Lawyers may rely on AI for document analysis or discovery, reducing their billable time and saving you legal fees.
  5. AI may reduce the emotional heat of negotiation. Some AI-assisted mediation platforms can propose settlement options and let people negotiate without every exchange escalating to a fight. But caution: Divorce is also a time when most people need a human to help develop options, since AI doesn’t know what really matters to you and your family. AI doesn’t know about knowledge or power imbalances in your marriage. A skilled mediator or divorce-trained mental health professional should be able to help you manage the conflict during the negotiations, as well as help you understand possible options for resolution.
  6. AI can produce scenarios around parenting time and spousal support. Using your work schedules and your children’s school schedules, AI can jump-start a process of creating a parenting plan. But caution: Decisions involving your children’s well-being are best developed with a divorce coach or trained mental health professional. AI may be able to calculate child support under your state guidelines, though spousal support is not generally formula-driven, and a human mediator or lawyer should be able to help you with those decisions.

Here are some serious AI risks you should know about.

  • AI can generate false evidence and cite nonexistent legal precedents. AI tries to please you and appease you with its friendly and authoritative tone, so it may generate disinformation. This could add to the conflict and confusion of your divorce process.
  • Another risk relates to privacy concerns when you upload private or sensitive financial or personal information to a web-based service. Most people prefer that their settlements be private, and this is one advantage of working with a human mediator or collaborative professional who will keep personal information out of court records.
  • Another risk is the over-reliance on AI for emotional and legal decisions, decisions that you will live with for many years ahead. Despite AI seeming almost human in its demeanor, this is deceptive. Remember that it is just an algorithm.
  • Finally, there is a risk that one spouse may access better tools or spend more money on AI resources, which might give them an unfair advantage.

AI can’t replace the human element. AI may streamline the mechanics and reduce some administrative costs, but divorce is much more about emotion, a sense of fairness, and future family relationships. AI may help lawyers, mediators, and judges shift away from paperwork to focus more on counsel. But their role is still essential when your divorce is more complicated financially, when you have children, or when there is more conflict. A human divorce professional can help you work through sensitive issues around parenting time, dividing assets, financial support, planning, and emotional recovery. AI can adopt an empathic tone and make you feel understood, supported, and encouraged. Remember to remind yourself that you cannot have a relationship with a machine!

So AI may be a valuable tool when used in conjunction with professional support. It may save some time and money, but it won’t ease the pain of divorce. The right professional guidance may do more to ease your passage through the divorce to emotional recovery.

item.title: 2 Habits That Make Your Life Dramatically Happier
item.description:
Happiness

2 Habits That Make Your Life Dramatically Happier

Incorporating these habits into your daily life can make you exponentially happier.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Research has shown that performing kindness activities reliably increased happiness.
  • Kindness as a daily habit can give rise to a greater sense of purpose, connection, and satisfaction with life.
  • Studies show that physical activity is consistently correlated with happiness across countries and regions.
Source: Allef Vinicius / Unsplash

The pursuit of happiness is a life journey that transcends borders, cultures, and language. For many people, it’s the one, singular thing we hope to achieve with our lives, if nothing else. We spend years searching for the right habit, mindset, or milestone that will finally bring us lasting happiness.

Yet at the same time, happiness can feel incredibly elusive. It’s portrayed in countless ways and associated with countless things. Money, family, career, love, success—we’re shown so many different paths to finding happiness. But after spending years chasing them down, many people discover they aren’t quite as happy as they imagined they’d be.

Part of the reason is that what constitutes happiness in one part of the world won’t necessarily translate to another. Western individualism versus broader collectivism, combined with the countless differences that make each person unique, makes it extraordinarily difficult to prescribe a single, universal path to happiness.

However, through decades of research and cross-cultural psychological studies, scientists have made remarkable progress in identifying several predictors of happiness that appear to transcend cultural boundaries. Below are two of them and how, regardless of who you are, incorporating them into your daily life can make you exponentially happier.

Habit 1: Be Kind

In a 2018 study published in The Journal of Social Psychology, researchers investigated whether a seven-day kindness activities intervention would increase individuals’ subjective happiness, specifically measuring whether different types of kindness activities had differential effects on happiness.

In the study, 683 participants from 29 different countries were asked to perform and observe acts of kindness for people they had either strong or weak social ties with, as well as to perform novel acts of self-kindness. Overall, the authors found that performing kindness activities for seven days reliably increased happiness. Additionally, they observed a positive correlation between the number of kind acts and increases in happiness.

What was perhaps most interesting is that the effects didn’t change across the different experimental groups. In other words, it didn’t matter whether the acts of kindness were directed to close friends, acquaintances, or oneself, or whether they were observed; kindness, in all its forms, had equally positive effects on happiness.

Simple acts of kindness don’t have to be massive, expensive undertakings. In fact, some of the most meaningful acts are often the simplest. Consider trying the following:

  • Send a thoughtful message to someone you haven’t spoken to in a while.
  • Offer a genuine compliment to a colleague, friend, or stranger.
  • Hold the door open for someone or help them carry something heavy.
  • Check in on a loved one who may be having a difficult week.
  • Leave a positive review for a small business you enjoy.
  • Donate books, clothes, or household items you no longer use.
  • Let someone merge into traffic or give up your place in a queue.
  • Perform an act of self-kindness, such as setting aside time to rest without guilt.

When integrated into your routine, kindness as a daily habit can give rise to a greater sense of purpose, connection, and satisfaction with life. These findings offer a much-needed sense of hope in that happiness isn’t something you have to wait to feel. Right now, at this very moment, you have the choice to actively create happiness through your treatment of yourself and others.

Habit 2: Move Your Body

Kindness demonstrates the power of our social nature. Physical activity, on the other hand, reflects the power hidden within our own biology. Among many other things, the human body evolved to move. And there’s a wealth of studies that show that our psychological well-being is very closely tied to that movement.

According to a 2018 systematic review published in the Journal of Happiness Studies, physical activity is consistently correlated with happiness across countries and regions. Of the more than 1,100 retrieved records, the researchers reviewed 15 observational studies (13 cross-sectional and two longitudinal) and eight intervention studies (six randomized controlled trials and two non-randomized trials).

Overall, the authors concluded that individuals only need as little as 10 minutes of physical activity per week—or one day of exercise per week—for increased levels of happiness. Two of the randomized controlled trials included older adults and even cancer survivors, and found that both aerobic exercise and stretching or balancing exercise were effective in improving happiness.

The good news is that benefiting from physical activity doesn’t require an expensive gym membership, specialized equipment, or elite athletic ability. Some accessible ways to get started include:

  • Taking a brisk walk around your neighborhood
  • Following a free yoga or stretching video online
  • Dancing to your favorite music in your living room
  • Taking the stairs instead of the elevator whenever possible
  • Going for a bike ride with friends or family
  • Doing a short bodyweight workout at home
  • Gardening, cleaning, or tackling physically active household tasks
  • Walking while taking phone calls instead of sitting down

The link between movement and happiness is driven by several factors at once. Physical activity stimulates the release of mood-enhancing neurotransmitters and endorphins that cause feelings of reduced stress and improved emotional well-being. Exercise can also improve sleep quality and boost energy levels, all while fostering a sense of accomplishment and reward.

It could be a walk through nature, a quick stretching session, or playing a sport competitively—regardless of the form, movement provides us with a welcome mental reset.

The most encouraging finding from the research is that the threshold for benefiting appears remarkably low. You don’t need to become a marathon runner or spend hours exercising each week. Small, consistent amounts of movement are enough to make a measurable difference to your happiness. And like kindness, physical activity works best when you make it a regular part of everyday life, rather than an occasional effort.

item.title: The Architecture of Awareness
item.description:
Meditation

The Architecture of Awareness

What research suggests about calm, clarity, and the trainable mind.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Brain wave research suggests that calm, clarity, and compassion are trainable.
  • Different brain waves — beta, alpha, and gamma — connect to different states of mind.
  • Different meditation styles evoke different brain waves.

Every state of mind has a rhythm. The brain is an electrical organ, and its neurons fire in collective waves that rise and fall at different speeds. Neuroscientists sort these into bands, and each band roughly corresponds to a different texture. Learning to notice these rhythms, and to shift among them, is one of the quieter offerings of contemplative practice. It moves meditation away from vague hope and toward something more like a craft.

Consider the spectrum. Beta waves, running from about 12 to 30 Hz, are the rhythm of ordinary waking life. Planning, analyzing, holding a conversation, getting the children to school. Beta is indispensable. But it has a shadow. When beta runs unchecked, it becomes the frequency of worry and threat-scanning, the inner narrator who will not stop. Much of modern life, with its notifications and deadlines, keeps us locked in agitated beta. That may be part of why so many people feel depleted without quite knowing why.

Alpha waves, from 8 to 12 Hz, are the first doorway out. Alpha arises when the mind relaxes but stays awake. It is the soft, spacious feeling just after you close your eyes, on a quiet walk, in calm and unfocused rest. Researchers sometimes describe it as relaxed readiness: alert but not contracted. Deeper still are theta waves, from 4 to 8 Hz, associated with dreamlike reverie and deep meditative absorption. Below those sit delta waves, under 4 Hz, the slow rhythm of dreamless, restorative sleep.

Then there is gamma. Gamma waves run from 30 to 100 Hz, with 40 Hz the most studied, and they are the fastest the brain produces. Where the slower bands represent degrees of quieting, gamma seems to represent the opposite, a heightening and an integration. It reflects large-scale neural synchrony, with distant regions of the brain firing together in coherent rhythm. Some researchers propose that gamma is part of how the brain binds scattered streams of sensation into a single field of experience. The idea is still debated, but it points to something intriguing: the possibility that clarity has a measurable signature.

This distinction matters for how we practice. Alpha is genuinely valuable. For a culture stranded in anxious beta, learning to drop into alpha is medicine. It lowers stress and restores the body. Many relaxation methods, and much of what passes for everyday mindfulness, aim here and stop. But alpha on its own is essentially calming. It quiets the noise. It does not, by itself, awaken anything new. A mind resting in pure alpha can be peaceful, dull, drowsy, or pleasantly blank.

Gamma represents a different aspiration. In research by Antoine Lutz, Richard Davidson, and colleagues, long-term Tibetan practitioners with tens of thousands of hours of training produced gamma oscillations of unusual amplitude and synchrony during open-presence and compassion practice. Their descriptions matched the physiology: heightened clarity, a vivid sense of non-separation, and effortless, panoramic knowing. This was not the strain of concentration. It read more like a wakeful brightness, alert and warm at once.

One finding stands out. The practitioners showed elevated gamma even at baseline, before they began meditating. Years of practice appeared to reshape the resting architecture of their minds. A passing state had, in some measure, become a lasting trait. Alpha is something you visit and leave, and it returns you to ordinary life largely unchanged. Gamma, cultivated over time, may shift the baseline itself, the person you are when you are not trying.

There is a caution worth noting. These were small samples of extraordinary practitioners, and correlation is not the same as causation. We do not yet know how much of the effect generalizes to ordinary people with ordinary schedules. Still, the direction is suggestive and runs against the romantic idea that luminous awareness belongs only to monks on mountaintops. The masters were not born with reorganized brains. They cultivated them.

In the deepest states, alpha and gamma appear together, spacious stillness and vivid clarity woven into one. That pairing echoes what contemplative traditions have long described, awareness that is open and knowing at the same time. And in the Lutz and Davidson work, compassion practice, not neutral calm, produced the strongest gamma. The open heart and the clear mind may not be two separate achievements.

If these capacities are trainable, they can be taught. One approach integrates three practices. Effortless mindfulness, in the lineage of Loch Kelly, invites a small shift from effortful attention to awake awareness, loosening the grip of beta. Mahamudra steadies that recognition, resting in an open, cognizant mind. Sustainable compassion practice, developed by John Makransky, opens the heart by receiving care and then extending it outward without burning out.

The research is early, and the mechanisms are uncertain. What seems clearer is the practical claim underneath it. Depth of this kind is not only given. It can be practiced, step by step, by people who are willing to try.
