item.title: When You Fear Happiness
item.description:
Anhedonia

When You Fear Happiness

Some people learn that joy can be dangerous: 4 causes; 4 solutions.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Not feeling happiness may be based on associating happiness with eventual disaster or self criticism.
  • People who struggle with feeling joy are often hypervigilant or overanalyzing, all driven by anxiety.
  • The antidotes are mindfulness, following preferences and excitement, and pushing against self criticism.
Source: besternchen / Pixabay

We know we can’t simply make ourselves happy or joyful. These feelings are byproducts of other things in our lives, such as good relationships, a satisfying job, and opportunities to be creative and use our talents. Yet some people say they never feel happy. They may know they should—others around them certainly do—but for them, those positive feelings never come.

4 Sources of Anhedonia

Such people would be clinically diagnosed with anhedonia, a lack of pleasure, but the label doesn’t explain its cause. Here are four common sources:

1. Growing up in an environment of depression and/or anxiety

If you had parents who were depressed or anxious, rarely happy, and always worrying or braced for the next bad thing, you may not only have inherited their temperament but also likely absorbed their view of life—that it is difficult, full of obstacles, and foreboding.

And if your parents were volatile and unable to provide the stability you needed, or if you suffered emotional or physical trauma, you likely learned to be hypervigilant to survive—always looking around corners, never relaxing into the moment, always on guard. As an adult, this software continues to run in the background, leaving you wired for anxiety, expecting the worst, and feeling vulnerable.

2. Being wired for caution

A famous line from a Tennyson poem reads: “'Tis better to have loved and lost than never loved at all.” Those who struggle with happiness would likely beg to differ: It’s better not to love or be happy than to risk losing them.

If you’re always expecting the worst, it makes sense that you might adopt a why-bother, pessimistic attitude and be leery of anything new, especially anything that seems emotionally risky. But the road to happiness often requires exactly that—risk—whether it’s taking on the challenge of a new job or calling up the person you met at the bar. By holding back on your life, you not only trade excitement for safety, but, more importantly, you never have the experience of finding out that what you think will happen—some disaster—never does. Only by stepping outside your comfort zone and having these corrective emotional experiences can you discover that life is not as scary as you always believed.

3. Being self-critical

The critical parent or bullying authority figure comes into your head, telling you that whatever you do is never good enough, that you should have always done better, and that you don’t deserve to be happy.

4. Overanalyzing and living in your head

Finally, there are those who live only in their heads, and their heads are always working overtime: analyzing, double- and triple-thinking, obsessing. Not only do they not feel joy, but they don’t feel much of anything: Thoughts drown out their emotions; they are essentially numb from the neck down. If you ask them how they feel, they may say they’re fine, but they really don’t know.

4 Ways to Rewire an Anhedonic Brain to Feel Joy

The theme is that for many good reasons, you’ve learned to distrust happiness, not seek or expect it, or associate it with anxiety and danger. But brain wiring can be changed. Here’s how to get started:

1. Cultivate preference, excitement, and passion

The antidote to anxiety is learning to approach it, which translates here to approaching positive emotions. Rather than avoiding, overanalyzing, or pushing positive feelings to the side, replace them with “positive spontaneity”—grasp the slightest wisp of positive emotion—a mere preference, an exciting idea, or, better still, a passion, no matter how small or seemingly minor. Next, run with that urge, image, or feeling—get that pizza for lunch, go play golf on a Saturday instead of cleaning the house, or call up the person you met at the bar. It’s not about pizza, golf, or a person, but about using feelings to tell you what you need. By going against your grain, you're pushing aside the feeling that a disaster is just around the corner.

2. Practice focusing on the present rather than the future

Life is only in the present, and you need to learn to spend less time in the future and more in the now. Easier said than done. You’ve been trained, by your overanalysis, hypervigilance, and caution, to try to control the future. Give it up. Life is made up of a series of nows, and your control is only over them. The more you can train your brain to be in the present, the less the future haunts you.

In practical terms, this means recognizing when you’re going down rabbit holes of anxiety. Say to yourself, “Here we go again; old stuff.” Recenter by stopping the runaway horse of your mind and focusing on your breathing, paying attention to the sights and sounds around you right now—mindfully cook, go for a walk, or engage your mind with a movie. Do something that pulls you out of the future and back to the present.

3. Meditation and medication

Research shows that meditation, in some form, can change your brain even if you do it for a few minutes a day. There are numerous websites to help you get started. Medication can help slow an overactive, anxious brain and reduce the noise and racing thoughts. Even in small doses, it can make a big difference. Talk to your health care provider about options.

4. Push back on self-criticism

Self-criticism kills joy. Time to push back against the bully. Start by recognizing when it kicks in and starts scolding you, and instead change the story: You did the best you could at the time, and you actually learned something new. Try treating yourself the way you would ideally treat a child you love who is being self-critical—letting them know it is OK, that mistakes are minor, and that life can be forgiving. By thinking this way, you’re treating yourself this way and getting now what you didn’t get when you were younger.

So, how to feel happiness? Cultivate preferences by acting on them; step outside your comfort zone to discover that you can trust your emotions and that the world is not as dangerous as you learned to believe. Rewire your brain by changing your self-talk and treating yourself now the way you weren’t treated as a child.

Happiness is nothing to fear.

item.title: What Developmental Histories Really Reveal
item.description:
Pregnancy

What Developmental Histories Really Reveal

Early experiences provide context, not blame, for understanding development.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Pregnancy experiences can shape early development but do not determine a child’s future.
  • Understanding early experiences can replace blame with compassion and insight.
  • Developmental histories help clinicians understand a child’s needs within their early life context.
Source: Gustavo Fring / Pexels

When I ask parents about their child’s earliest beginnings, there is often a pause.

Sometimes it is brief—dates, scans, milestones recalled with ease. But sometimes it lingers. In that pause, something more complex surfaces: uncertainty, grief, exhaustion, or even relief at finally being asked.

Over time, I have learned not to rush it.

Because developmental histories are often treated as a structured part of neurodevelopmental assessments—questions about pregnancy, birth, early milestones, communication, and behaviour—but in practice, they are something much more human.

They are an attempt to understand how a child’s story unfolded long before they arrive in a clinic room.

And that story rarely begins at birth.

It begins in the emotional, physical, and social environment that surrounds their earliest development (Aldinger et al., 2024).

What Is a Developmental History?

In the United Kingdom, neurodevelopmental assessments and developmental histories are used to build a picture of how a child has grown over time, particularly when autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or learning differences are being explored.

On paper, it can look like a checklist. In reality, it rarely feels like one.

We ask about pregnancy, birth, early milestones, language development, social interaction, behaviour, and family context. But what we are really trying to understand is not just what a child is doing now, but how they came to be this way.

Importantly, developmental histories are not about assigning blame or locating a single cause. They are about context.

They help clinicians understand development as a process shaped by multiple interacting influences over time, including biology, environment, relationships, and lived experience (Zong et al., 2025).

Every Family Has a Different Beginning

Some beginnings carry a quieter but significant form of pain that is not always visible in clinical settings. For some parents, conception itself has been shaped by infertility, repeated loss, or the emotional and physical demands of IVF, with cycles of hope and disappointment that sit just outside the clinical narrative.

For others, the child’s arrival may not involve biological pregnancy at all. Adoptive parents, foster carers, and those through donor conception or surrogacy may describe a different kind of beginning—one that can include longing, uncertainty, or complex feelings about identity and belonging, alongside love and commitment.

These experiences are important in developmental histories not because they determine outcomes but because they shape the emotional context in which a child is received and understood.

What These Conversations Often Reveal

Although developmental histories are structured, what emerges are stories.

Parents talk about waiting for scan results and fearing the unknown. About fertility journeys marked by repeated loss. About pregnancies shaped by financial stress, migration, relationship difficulties, or simply trying to get through each day.

Others describe quieter emotional experiences.

“I was anxious throughout the pregnancy.”

“I didn’t feel connected at first.”

“I was just surviving.”

These are not minor details. They describe the environment in which development began.

Research suggests that prenatal experiences, including maternal stress, can influence aspects of child development. However, these influences are neither direct nor deterministic (Aldinger et al., 2024; Zong et al., 2025).

They form part of a much larger developmental picture, rather than defining it.

Culture, Meaning, and Pregnancy

Growing up in an Indian cultural context, I became aware early on that pregnancy is never experienced as purely biological.

Beliefs, advice, and cultural narratives surround it.

I remember hearing things like: “Drink milk, and the baby will be fairer,” “Eat certain foods for a good baby,” or “Stay positive because your emotions affect the baby.”

Whether or not these beliefs are supported by evidence, they reflect something important: Pregnancy is often seen as a deeply influential period in which the mother’s actions carry meaning for the child’s future.

These narratives are not unique to one culture. Across societies, pregnancy is shaped by expectations—sometimes comforting, sometimes pressurising, and often deeply internalised.

For clinicians, understanding this cultural context is essential. It helps us recognise not only what families experienced but also how they interpret those experiences.

Understanding Without Blame

One of the most important distinctions in developmental work is between understanding and assigning causation.

Research does show that early environments, including prenatal experiences, can contribute to developmental outcomes. At the same time, no single factor determines a child’s trajectory (Zong et al., 2025).

Development is shaped over time through interactions between genetics, caregiving, environment, relationships, and opportunity.

This is why developmental histories are not about identifying what went “wrong.”

They are about understanding what happened.

This distinction matters, particularly for parents who arrive carrying guilt or self-blame. Many worry that something they did during pregnancy or early parenting caused their child’s difficulties.

More often than not, what emerges is a different realisation: that they were navigating complex circumstances with the resources they had at the time.

Listening Beyond the Checklist

No developmental history is perfect.

Some are detailed; others contain gaps, uncertainty, or unanswered questions. Clinicians are not looking for flawless recall. They are looking for understanding.

Sometimes these conversations change how a child is seen. Behaviours that once appeared isolated begin to make sense within a broader developmental story.

Sometimes parents begin to see themselves differently, too—not as having failed, but as people who were doing their best within difficult circumstances.

Every developmental history begins before diagnosis, before assessment, and before labels.

It begins with context.

When we take the time to listen to that context with curiosity rather than judgment, we move beyond explanation toward understanding.

And in that shift, both children and their families are often seen a little more clearly.

item.title: Intermarriage on America's 250th Birthday
item.description:
Race and Ethnicity

Intermarriage on America's 250th Birthday

Intermarriage was illegal for much of our history. Now one in six newlyweds intermarry.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • We have come a long way in the number of intermarriages and in our acceptance of them.
  • Intermarried couples generally feel optimistic about the future of intermarriage.
  • Challenges still arise and these couples often carefully select where they live and with whom they socialize.

As we turn the page on our first 250 years as a country, it is remarkable how far we have come in terms of intermarriage. Marriage between Black people and white people was banned in many colonies (later states) as well as between other races. It was only 59 years ago, in the 1967 Loving Supreme Court Decision, that intermarriage was finally legalized nationally at a time when many southern states still banned it. Today, one in ten marriages is interracial or interethnic (between Hispanic/Latinos and non-Hispanic/Latinos). Asian Americans and Hispanic/Latino Americans are most likely to intermarry and Whites are the least likely.

In our 2026 book, Interracial marriage: How diverse couples navigate relationships in a divided time, Victoria Stubbs, Michael Woolley and I document that many couples are doing well in their marriages, rate them highly, and are optimistic about the future for interethnic and interracial marriages. At the same time, and at a period in our history where hate crimes based on race and ethnicity are still being recorded at a high level, a number of couples are also looking over their shoulder and have arranged their lives to avoid uncomfortable situations that mono-racial and mono-ethnic couples do not avoid.

These couples are part of the wave of newlyweds intermarrying, now one in six. Not surprisingly, if they are living in a diverse neighborhood or city, they feel more comfortable. Many have carefully chosen where to live, what social groups to join and what social groups to avoid, and where to vacation. Attendance at family events may be curated based on how accepted they feel with each other's family. While immediate family members are usually accepting, more distant ones may be less so.

Mixed-race children are more comfortable in their social environments as their numbers increase, consistent with the increase in intermarriage. Challenges do remain for some, as children may not look like either parent and may not look like each other. Identity formation, often a challenge for every tween and teen, may change based on what social group and possibly what racial group identity they choose. Some mixed-race children seek out others who have the same mixed-race identity.

Racial perspective-taking is one tried and true approach for these families and for us as a nation. They, and we, must listen to each other, inquire about race-related experiences without challenging, and accept that perspectives may differ based on racial history and gender identity. Stereotypes generally become less invidious if we get to know people who we may stereotype. So, let's begin to listen in "stereo" as interracial couples and families, who are making their marriages work, are doing. They have triumphed over difference and we must also.

item.title: Holistic Hybrid Health: Why It Starts From the Inside Out
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Holistic Hybrid Health: Why It Starts From the Inside Out

Double literacy as a critical well-being factor.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Increasingly, we think with technology, feel through it, choose inside it, and compare ourselves through it.
  • Meaningful friction is the space from which capacity arises.
  • Environmental sustainability is a health prerequisite.
Holistic hybrid health begins from the inside out—with aspirations, emotions, thoughts, and bodily sensations. It is nurtured from the outside in.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI, 2026

A child asks a homework app to explain photosynthesis. A manager asks artificial intelligence (AI) to draft feedback. A mother scrolls through sleep advice. A teenager keeps refreshing a feed that knows his soft spot. An older adult types symptoms into a chatbot. Together, these moments form a new well-being environment.

Health is still shaped by food, movement, sleep, medicine, and social support. Yet another layer runs through impulse, attention, and action: algorithmic mediation. Increasingly, we think with technology, feel through it, choose inside it, and compare ourselves through it.

That is why we need a framework for human health: holistic hybrid health (HHH). It begins from the inside out, with aspirations, emotions, thoughts, and bodily sensations. It is nurtured from the outside in, through relationships, institutions, technology, and the planet. Its guiding question: In a world designed to predict behavior, how do we help people make their own best choices and protect agency?

Why the first vital sign is agency

Agency is the ability to act from one’s own attention, judgment, values, and intention. It is the capacity to pause before reacting, notice what is influencing us, and choose in a way that feels ours. A 2025 Microsoft Research study on generative AI and critical thinking collected hundreds of workplace examples. It found that critical thinking depended on the task, user self-confidence, and confidence in the AI system. When people trusted the machine too much, or themselves too little, thinking deteriorated.

The lesson is to preserve the space of the self while using AI. Arrogance about one’s own skills and self-depreciation create vulnerability. Overestimating or undervaluing our abilities makes us easier prey for over-reliance. Hybrid humility is the counterpart of HHH.

The brain needs meaningful friction

A frictionless life sounds attractive until we remember how capacity grows. The brain develops through effort, attention, repair, memory, and practice. Muscles need resistance. Judgment does too.

Imagine a student who uses AI to summarize every reading before reading. She may perform better. Over time, she becomes less patient with ambiguity, less able to follow a difficult argument, and less confident in her interpretation. A 2025 randomized controlled trial on ChatGPT found that students using ChatGPT as a study aid performed worse on a surprise retention test 45 days later than students using traditional methods.

Meaningful friction is the space from which capacity arises. The sharper question is: What is the screen replacing, and what dependency is forming? One soft spot is compulsive use: feeling unable to stop, distressed away from a device, or driven to escape problems through it. Technology can connect or consume, educate or agitate, support agency or weaken it.

Double literacy: the new life skill

The first part is human literacy: understanding oneself as a whole person. What am I aspiring to? What emotion is present? What thought keeps repeating? What is my body telling me? A headache before a meeting, tightness before sending a message, or an urge to check the phone after rejection: These are data from the inside.

The second part is algorithmic literacy: understanding how digital systems influence attention, emotion, behavior, and belief. Why am I seeing this? What is being optimized? What does this tool make easier? What does it make unnecessary? Which part of me does it reward: curiosity, fear, vanity, generosity, impatience?

Consider a person searching for fitness advice. The feed may offer routines, body comparisons, supplement ads, and influencers who turn insecurity into revenue. Lack of self-value is commodified. Human literacy helps the person listen to their body and examine habits. Algorithmic literacy helps them ask: Does this system profit from keeping me engaged rather than well? Does this forum trigger anxiety, or provide comfort? Double literacy turns a passive target into a proactive participant.

Health also comes from the outside in

Inner awareness cannot protect a human from harmful external conditions. A child cannot meditate their way out of unsafe housing. A worker cannot gratitude-journal their way out of chronic heat exposure. A community cannot breathe well if the air is polluted.

This is why HHH must include planetary health. The 2025 Planetary Health Check reported that seven of nine planetary boundaries have now been breached, with ocean acidification added for the first time. The 2025 Lancet Countdown warned that climate-related health impacts are worsening, while the World Health Organization’s 2026 update on heat and health states that heatwaves and prolonged excess heat are increasing in frequency, duration, intensity, and magnitude.

Environmental sustainability is a health prerequisite. Heat changes sleep. Sleep changes mood. Mood changes conflict. Conflict changes families. Families shape children. Children become societies. Planetary stress enters the body, household, classroom, clinic, and workplace. A healthy hybrid human needs a habitable planet. Personal well-being is conditioned by planetary health.

A practical takeaway: your holistic hybrid health halt

Today we are building the behavioral architecture in which future humans will develop their minds and bodies. Agency deserves recognition as a public health priority and personal practice. Once a day, before using AI, opening a feed, answering a difficult message, or making a health-related choice, make an HHH halt.

Ask four questions.

  1. What is happening inside me? Name one aspiration, one emotion, one thought, and one physical sensation.
  2. What is shaping me from the outside in? Notice the platform, person, room, incentive, stressor, or environmental condition influencing the moment.
  3. Am I tempted to accept external guidance without internal thought? Yes or no, and why?
  4. What choice will strengthen my agency? Choose the action that leaves you more empowered than simple algorithmic adoption.

For the student, that means reading the original paragraph before asking AI for help. For the mother, putting the phone outside the bedroom. For the manager, drafting the hard message personally, using AI to refine tone. For the teenager, replacing one late-night scroll with a voice note to a friend. For the health seeker, calling a clinician when symptoms matter.

Holistic hybrid health begins in that halt. It is the moment where the self is allowed to return to itself.

item.title: Why You Don't Need to Be Loud to Be Defiant
item.description:
Conformity

Why You Don't Need to Be Loud to Be Defiant

Defiance is not a personality trait. It is a practice anyone can build.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Most people overestimate how readily they would speak up when it matters.
  • People comply with bad advice even when they know it is bad because saying no is hard.
  • Defiance is not a personality trait but a practice that anyone can build.
Silence as a social pressure, not a personal failing.
Source: AI-Generated

Most of us, in the abstract, believe we would push back when we see something is wrong. We picture ourselves as the one who would object, refuse, or stand up when others sat down. Decades of research suggest we are wrong. But the same research, paradoxically, contains good news.

When I was seven years old, walking home with my mother in West Yorkshire, England, a group of teenage boys blocked our path in a narrow alleyway. One of them yelled, "Go back home." My quiet, conflict-avoiding mother stopped, turned, and asked, calmly, "What do you mean?" When the boys didn't answer, she asked her question again.

I have spent most of my adult life trying to understand what she did. Not because the moment was loud or dramatic. It was not. She did something most of us, in most situations, never do. She closed a gap that most of us don't even realize we have.

It is the gap between what we believe we would do, and what we actually do, when something is wrong.

The Gap Is Bigger Than You Think

Ask people in the abstract whether they would object to a clearly bad decision, refuse to participate in something unethical, or push back against a senior colleague who crossed a line. Most will say yes. Of course they would.

Decades of research, including mine, suggest otherwise.

In study after study, I have found high levels of compliance with bad advice, even when people know the advice is bad and face no consequences for refusing it (Sah, et al. 2013, 2019; Sah, 2025).

In one experiment, participants chose between two lottery options, A and B. Lottery A was clearly superior, with prizes worth more than twice as much as B's. When participants chose on their own, more than 95 percent picked A. But when a stranger recommended Lottery B, the decision flipped. Participants increasingly followed the recommendation they could see was inferior. In one condition, compliance with the stranger's bad advice rose to over 80 percent. They had full information. There were no consequences for disagreeing. They followed the advice anyway.

When asked, they reported being less pleased with their choice and trusting the advice less. They knew the advice was bad. They followed it because saying no in someone's presence is harder than knowing the right answer.

The Gap Is More Closable Than You Think

Here is the part that gets less attention. The same research that shows how compliant we can be also shows what closes the gap.

In my research, when participants made their decision in private, away from the advisor, compliance dropped dramatically. And when participants made a public choice in front of the advisor and were then given a chance to revisit it alone, 43 percent of those who had initially complied changed their minds. Their public decision and their private decision were not the same decision.

What changed was not the information. What changed were the conditions.

What Closes the Gap

The question is not whether we are the brave kind of person or the silent kind. Most of us are far more silent than we imagine we are. But we are also closer to speaking up than the bleakness of these findings might suggest.

What closes the gap is not personality. It is conditions and practice. A single ally. A workplace norm that push-back is welcome and expected. A previous moment when we tried something small and survived. A pause before answering. A decision made in private rather than in the room.

Speaking at TEDxNew England on closing the gap between belief and action.
Source: Sunita Sah

In my TEDx talk, How to Stand Up For Yourself and Others, I tell the full story of my mother and what I learned from her about closing the gap. The talk introduces a tool called the Defiance Compass (Sah, 2025), built around three deliberate questions that help us figure out when and how to speak up when it matters.

This is what my mother had built, in ways I did not see as a child. Not bravado, not loudness, not the personality of someone who could be expected to stand up to a group of teenage boys in an alleyway. Something else: the habit of having done so, in smaller moments, in private, on her own terms, until the moment in the alleyway arrived and the habit was there.

The gap is bigger than we think. And it is more closable than we think. Both of these things are true, and the practical implication is the same. The work of speaking up does not begin in the moment when speaking up is hard. It begins long before.

item.title: The "Let Them" Theory: Therapeutic Wisdom or Pop Psychology?
item.description:
Wisdom

The "Let Them" Theory: Therapeutic Wisdom or Pop Psychology?

The origins of the "let them" theory in ancient philosophy.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Practicing Mel Robbins' "Let Them Theory" can relieve suffering.
  • The theory helps people let go of painful feelings.
  • The wisdom of the "let them" theory has roots in ancient Stoic philosophy.

The Let Them Theory by author and podcaster Mel Robbins may be the latest viral self-help craze that people discount as “pop” psychology. But the “let them” theory actually offers a powerful tool for the therapist’s toolbox and a potentially powerful guide to achieving inner peace. Simple on the surface but rooted in age-old wisdom, the ability to “let them” frees people from unnecessary suffering. But letting go of what we can’t control is not easy. “Let them” requires us to rise above natural feelings like jealousy, envy, anger, and the need to control others. Needless to say, reaching the “let them” state of mind requires discipline, practice, and mindfulness. Reading the book carefully, and even more than once, can provide guidance toward a peaceful state of mind if the reader is open to it.

If someone has a nicer car or house then you do, then “let them,” Robbins advises. Instead of dwelling on what others have and we don’t and feeling envy, the theory advises us to think about what is important and meaningful in our own lives. Here are some of Robbins’s examples: If a friend betrays you, rather than being eaten up by feelings of sadness and anger, the healthier attitude is to “let them.” Then empower yourself by being open to new friends who elevate you and bring out your best nature. Instead of feeling needy and demanding when your spouse is away on a business trip, tell yourself, "Let them,” and pursue what gives meaning to your own life.

Robbins calls the second part of the “Let them” theory “Let me.” Rather than dwelling on external events that cause us pain, the “let me” part of the theory leads us to empower ourselves. For example, in a therapy session Elliot explained that he felt anxiety when his wife Alice traveled for business or when she went on an occasional girls’ weekend. He was angry at her if she didn’t call or text him several times a day. Alice explained that she was always busy on her trips. She didn’t always have the privacy for a phone call or even a text more than once a day in the evening. Elliot was retired and didn’t have enough to fill the void in his life. In therapy, we discussed the need to fill the void with things other than his wife. Over the weeks, Elliot joined a hiking group and a pickleball group. He also started volunteering twice a week with a green energy group. Filling his days with activities that he enjoyed allowed him freedom from anxiety when Alice was travelling. Finally, he was able to “let her.” If a daily phone call was all that Alice could manage when she was away, then he was content with that.

The wisdom of the “Let them” theory is ancient in origin. It is the essence of a school of philosophy called Stoicism, which flourished in ancient Greece and Rome two thousand years ago. The wisdom of letting go of what is not in our control was articulated by a disabled Greek slave in Rome named Epictetus. Although a slave, Epictetus was allowed to study philosophy and later became known as one of the great Stoic philosophers. There is only one way to achieve happiness, taught Epictetus: Let go of things that are not in our control. What is in our control us is our ability to adjust our attitude toward external things. As a slave, Epictetus had little control over external events and other people’s actions in the material world. But he had a powerful mind, which empowered him to adjust his thoughts and attitude in the spiritual, psychological, and mental realms.

Stoicism is often thought of as a philosophy of detachment from the world. In fact, Stoicism teaches detachment from our reactions to external things that cause us anxiety and unhappiness. Stoicism taught that it is not external reality that causes anxiety and unhappiness. Rather, it is our mental attitude or thoughts about the external world. We cannot change external reality but we can change our ways of thinking about it and attain peace of mind. For the Stoics, happiness did not reside in the ownership of material things or achieving a powerful position. Instead, they taught, happiness is a state of inner peace.

item.title: Rewilding and Slow Watching Offer Windows Into Animal Minds
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Rewilding and Slow Watching Offer Windows Into Animal Minds

It's essential to rekindle cognitive ethology.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Now more than ever we need details on what wild animals think and feel about what's happening in their lives.
  • Comparative studies of animal minds show we're not the only show in town concerning sentience.
  • We must get over ourselves, pay attention to science, and coexist with other animals.
Looking for dingoes in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, Australia.
Source: Brad Purcell/with permission.

Professional researchers with varying backgrounds and interests study animal behavior. For the most part, these include biologists. ethologists, psychologists, and anthropologists who observe animals under different circumstances and with different interests. Many researchers also study animals but spend little to no time actually watching the creatures in whom they're interested. These include philosophers and those people interested in the broad transdisciplinary field called animal studies.

All of these people can contribute to learning more about these amazing beings, but there is no substitute for carefully observing—"slow watching"—the nonhumans in which they're keenly interested. These data and stories are crucial for learning who these beings truly are —for "minding them"—and for appreciating what their capacities for behavioral flexibility and highly evolved levels of consciousness tell us about how they think and feel about how their lives can change because of the behavior of members of the same species and other species, including humans, and what they think and feel about intrusions into their heads, hearts, and homes.1

What is ethology?

Ethology is the study of animal behavior. It focuses mainly on wild animals in their natural habitats, although some ethological work has involved captive animals. In 1973, ethologists Konrad Lorenz, Niko Tinbergen, and Karl von Frisch shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine for their discoveries related to animal behavior.

Here I am, riding my field vehicle looking for animals on the sidewalks of Brooklyn when I was 3 years old.
Source: Marc Bekoff.

I've been an ethologist since I was around three years of age and even was "minding" animals" without even knowing. I've continued to do so for more than 50 years in that I carefully watch—patiently slow watch—animals, primarily if not exclusively in their natural habitats. During the last few years, more and more people have asked me what ethology is and what do ethologists do because these words are increasingly appearing in discussions of animal behavior even in popular media.

Ethologists have always thought that behavior is but one way in which animals speak to us. Following up on Nobel laureate Niko Tinbergen's classic work in ethology, in which he stressed that studies of behavior should center on four areas of inquiry, namely, evolution, adaptation, causation, and ontogeny (development), in an essay called "Amending Tinbergen: A fifth aim for ethology," Gordon Burghardt added a fifth area he called "private experience" to Tinbergen's list. In addition, Dale Jamieson and I wrote a paper called "On Aims and Methods of Cognitive Ethology" in which we showed just how fruitful and influential Tinbergen's work has been in the study of animal minds, although he didn't do this sort of research. Today, numerous ethologists have noted that we must learn about and appreciate animal minds and what's in them, hence the enormous growth of cognitive ethology.

The significant contributions of cognitive ethology

Cognitive ethology refers specifically to the study of animal minds—what’s in them and how they work, their thoughts and feelings. My own research has focused on the study of animal minds, including their cognitive and emotional capacities.

Cognitive ethologists want to know what it is like to be another animal. What is their lived experience from their point of view? What do they see, hear, and smell? Why do they do what they do? Empirical scientific evidence combined with common sense and intuition is all it takes to get a pretty reliable picture of who animals are and what they want and need.

Following Tinbergen's suggestions, ethologists are also interested in other important questions: How and why have emotions and behaviors evolved? How do animals adapt their behaviors to succeed in a changing situation or environment and what causes them to do so? How do behaviors develop within an individual or society?

Flexibility of behavior—the ability to change your response when things around you change—also is important because it's a sign of awareness, or what scientists call a mark of consciousness. This shows that an animal is thinking and acting with intention, not instinct. The animal is evaluating their situation, considering past experiences, and deciding what to do based on the present moment and imagined future situations.

What goes around comes around

For far too many years, people interested in animal minds were considered to be on the fringes of "real science" because we can't really ever know what nonhumans are thinking and feeling. How wrong they have turned out to be.

What goes around comes around and currently, the fields of ethology and cognitive ethology are rapidly growing in terms of the number of researchers engaged in this sort of research and also in the scope of the species they study and the questions they ask.1 This is because the data they generate are highly relevant to what's happening in the minds and hearts of these animals.

When I think about what it takes to collect detailed data on the behavior of other animals that bear on their abilities to think and feel, I immediately understand we must get over ourselves and I think of what I call "Soft Personal Rewilding"—deeply connecting with nature as we study these animals because it's often easy, cheap, and accessible. What could be better? Formal research in these areas also can be far less costly than studies that depend on studying captive animals who might not be able to express what they know and what they're thinking and feeling where they're being studied.

Cognitive ethology expands the biodiversity of sentience and consciousness

Learning about the behavior, minds, and hearts of other animals surely is an eclectic endeavor. The fascinating array of animals in whom we're interested, the incredibly diverse patterns of behavior they display, and the enormous range of the problems nonhumans faced clearly and forcefully argue for a broad transdisciplinary approach in which people work together, as we move on toward peaceful coexistence and the end of horrific global animal abuse once and for all.

These animals display the biodiversity of sentience.
Source: Danielle Calibird Fernandez/with permission.

When we pay careful attention to what other animals are telling us about what they want, need, think, and feel and do something about it's a win-win for all. In a book called Saving Animals, Saving Ourselves, NYU's Dr. Jeff Sebo argues that ample science shows what harms them (other animals) also harms us and we must pay close attention to this important and unavoidable double-edged sword.

It's time to celebrate animal sentience and stop squabbling. Animal sentience isn’t science fiction. and the important question is not if sentience has evolved but why.

We can, and we must do better. Solid science—cognitive ethology, evolutionary biology, comparative psychology, animal studies—and a dose of common sense can lead the way. Surely, it's time to stop wondering if other animals are sentient—they clearly are. Cognitive ethology can clearly lead the way.

item.title: Trust: Have We Lost Our Faith in Others?
item.description:
Trust

Trust: Have We Lost Our Faith in Others?

Trust is a reciprocal affair that requires social solutions.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Public trust is a shared belief that people will act in orderly, mutually respectful ways.
  • Research indicates that trust in business, government, religion, and other people has fallen.
  • Addressing distrust means understanding its causes and building models of public responsibility.

“In God We Trust.” On July 11, 1955, President Eisenhower signed legislation directing that all American coins and currency would henceforth carry that designation. A check of one’s wallet or purse will reveal that this is indeed the case. Even the humble penny, now retired, makes clear that commercial trading has, ultimately, the sanctioning power of the sacred.

The context for this change was the Cold War with the Soviet Union, which was seen as the bastion of godless totalitarianism. America, it was felt, needed to affirm its spiritual foundations. For similar reasons, the phrase “under God” was added to the Pledge of Allegiance on Flag Day (June 14) the year before.

Of course, there were opponents of the new language, who argued that our country’s founders had been emphatic that, and in contrast to England, church and state should remain separate. To be sure, freedom to believe, including religious freedom, must be protected by government. However, no specific version of belief should have the imprimatur of officialdom. Moreover, if our country is to survive its shaky beginnings, we must look to one another for support. Formerly separate colonies must stand together and relinquish some of their independence. The power of the wealthy must be tempered by democratic processes. The resounding theme of the American experiment is the centrality of “we the people.”

Those of us who grew up in the 1950s remember well the post-war commitments to nuclear families, long-term employer-employee relationships, home ownership, suburbs, and automobiles. Churches, like schools and office buildings, were markers of community prosperity. Religious faith was linked to business success, civic mindedness, and patriotism.

The sociologist and religious scholar Robert Bellah called that mixture of belief America’s “civil religion,” essentially a broad acknowledgment that public life is anchored by a vaguely defined but supervening God who cares for us as a people. In that spirit, prayer and religious symbols were commonly inserted into sport events and community meetings. And the nation itself was granted quasi-religious significance, with an assemblage of sacred texts, heroes and martyrs, rituals, and holidays.

Have we lost belief in the constancy and benevolence of such arrangements? This post explores that theme.

What does it mean to “trust”?

The psychotherapist Erik Erikson argued that developing a sense of trust is the first psychological challenge in human development. Infants need to know that the world is an orderly place featuring identifiable individuals who care for them. Pointedly, infants cannot perform these activities by themselves. The foundations of trust lie beyond the person.

Most of us carry these expectations through life. When we come home from work, we anticipate our residence to be much as it was when we left it, filled by accustomed people acting in accustomed ways. We want our possessions to be in their usual places. When we look in the mirror, we trust that our visage will resemble the person we saw that morning.

That web of expectations spreads across society. Work environments, neighborhoods, local stores, doctors’ offices, and the like must be places we can count on. Indeed, we are willing to trust that complete strangers, such as taxi drivers and food deliverers, will treat us as they should.

Without that sense of familiarity, we cannot act—or think and feel—with confidence. Without trust, social relationships (essentially, the uncountable interchanges of organizations and individuals) cannot function.

However, sheer stability of expectations is not enough. After all, we may be confident that a person we know is going to act in a rude or intemperate way just as they did yesterday. That isn’t trust. Instead, and for most scholars, trust contains the idea that people are essentially pro-social and that we can depend on them to respect us and to uphold their end of the bargains we make with them. Few of us have the probity of the 12-year-old Anne Frank, who believed until the end that people are basically “good at heart,” but most have concluded that we must rely on others.

Whom do we trust?

Most psychological writing on trust focuses on relationships with people we know well: family, friends, and co-workers. But trust is more than that.

I began this post with a remembrance of the 1950s attempt to institutionalize trust in God. It will not surprise the reader to be informed that this trust has declined. According to the Pew Research Center, only about half (54%) of Americans now are “absolutely certain” that God exists. This 2023 finding compares to the 71% who made this claim as recently as 2007. Although most adults (79%) believe there is “something spiritual beyond the natural world,” there is little agreement about how this spirituality operates as a motive force in individuals' lives or in the world more generally.

Do we trust business, that presumed anchor of American prosperity? According to 2024 research by Forbes magazine, most business executives (90%) think their customers “highly trust” their companies, but only 30% of those consumers do so. Similarly, 79% of consumers believe that businesses will fail to use AI responsibly. And few now believe corporate claims of transparency and public service.

Public trust in government is at historic lows. Pew Researchers report that in 1958 73% of adults felt they could trust government to “do the right thing” at least “most of the time.” In 2025, that figure had fallen to just 17%. Even for those who support the party in power, there is a sense that Washington politicians are incompetent, cowardly, or self-serving.

Most distressing is a loss of faith in people at large. In 1972, 46% of adults said that “most people can be trusted.” This fell to 34% in the 2023-24 Pew Research Center poll. Consistently, and as many others have reported, we are less likely to know our neighbors, belong to churches, or participate in community organizations than earlier generations.

Why do we distrust?

Trust levels are higher when people live in stable communities where they interact with one another in regular, courteous, face-to-face ways. Such beliefs are aided by public messaging—from media and social leaders—which stresses the good deeds of ordinary citizens. Most importantly, residents must feel that the community or society supports people like themselves and has their interests at heart. Predictably, those who are white and wealthy tend to have higher trust than poor people and minorities.

Because an increasing portion of interaction now occurs at a “distance,” that is, via electronic media, most of us know little of the persons—if they are persons—we deal with. Bureaucracies, both in business and government, have become gigantic. Wealth has become concentrated in a very small segment of the population, which lives in gated communities. Corporations are driven by the profit demands of shareholders. Media reporting stresses the corruption and blundering of executives and public officials.

Pointedly, trust is a reciprocal affair, which relies on mutual exchanges of goodwill. Lapsing into cynicism or private scheming will not address the problem. Neither will quiescence toward the malpractices of large organizations. Public trust depends on educating ourselves about the matters at hand, holding others accountable, and supporting leaders who maintain a vision of public responsibility.

item.title: Opening the Door to the Subconscious
item.description:
Unconscious

Opening the Door to the Subconscious

How to release conscious control with silence and awe.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • There are key differences between inner quiet and outer silence.
  • When we feel awe our focus on ourselves diminishes.
  • The subconscious is oriented towards feelings and images more than towards words.
Source: Berni0004/Shutterstock

The conscious mind thrives on stimulation from inputs like language, sound, comparisons, and problem solving. When sensory and cognitive input decreases—when we become quiet—we make room for subconscious regulation and guidance.

It’s not a coincidence that so many of our quietest practices—prayer, meditation, time spent in nature—are also the practices we can use to feel a sense of peace and calm.

Interestingly, there are key differences between inner quiet and outer silence. Outer silence—the absence of environmental noise—sometimes makes us feel more alert rather than less (Donnelly, 2023).

For people unaccustomed to stillness, this kind of quiet may feel uncomfortable at first, like your mind is scanning for threats. If you feel this way when you're trying to achieve calm, that's not a failure. Consider it conditioning; with routine and practice the quiet will become familiar and embraced by your mind.

The goal, of course, is inner quiet. When mental noise decreases and tension settles, the nervous system shifts away from vigilance. Human cultures recognized this reality long before neuroscience could describe it. Moments of silence, contemplative prayer, monastic practices, and days of rest all create conditions in which conscious driving recedes and deeper regulation emerges.

Nature, Awe, and Feeling Small

A powerful way to relinquish conscious control and open communication with the subconscious is through experiences that make us feel both small and part of something vast.

One of my 20-year-old patients, Sophia, reported experiencing a life-changing vision from her subconscious that gave her this feeling. In her freshman year of college, she fell asleep in her dorm. During her nap, she felt her soul move out of her body and toward a ball of energy and light, which she then entered.

Inside that energy, she envisioned the world from its very beginning—the Big Bang, the origin of Earth, the sprouting of the first tree, the ages of fish and dinosaurs and mammals. She witnessed storms and fires and tectonic plates shifting—all from a great distance where she felt safe and clear in the knowing that everything was happening as it should be.

When the vision ended, my patient felt disoriented. She did not recognize her room or even her own hands. But she heard the voice of her subconscious, soothing and calm, telling her who she was and where she’d been. Later, when we asked her subconscious why Sophia had this experience, it replied, I wanted to show her a bigger life.

Her guided, awe-filled tour of the universe did just that, by showing Sophia how much she is an integral part of something vast and wonderful.

Interestingly, the use of psychedelics in supervised therapy sometimes elicits a similar sense to what Sophia experienced. Patients report feeling a temporary loss of their sense of self and a blurring of the boundaries between themselves and the world. Many describe feeling unity with other people, with nature, and with the cosmos. These awe-filled experiences can broaden our mindsets and allow us to feel part of something bigger (Soylemez, 2025).

When we feel awe—perhaps when we view a sweeping landscape, a night sky, or the expansiveness of the ocean—our focus on ourselves diminishes. These things make us feel small in the best possible way—small because we’re part of something vast and beautiful and cohesive. When we feel this way, our immediate concerns shrink. Our perception of time can even soften.

Among my patients who've mastered the skill of allowing the subconscious take over, many report losing any sense of passing time. Ten minutes in hypnosis, for example, might feel like hours of calm contemplation.

Awe, like outer silence, is not the goal. Rather, it’s a pathway to feelings of peace and calm, which allows us to better interact with our inner selves.

Communication with the Subconscious

The subconscious communicates differently than the conscious mind. Our conscious minds lean heavily on language. Words are our way of defining our circumstances. The subconscious, however developed long before language, and is more oriented towards feelings and images than towards words (LeDoux, 1996).

Many of my patients who have directly communicated with their subconscious have felt limited by, and even expressed frustration with, the limitations that come with having to capture big feelings or concepts in words.

The sense I get is not that these people lack the ability to use language, but rather that language itself is a limiting tool. Imagine a composer being asked to work at a piano with only ten keys instead of the standard 88, and you begin to grasp the inherent disparity between the vastness of the human experience and the narrowness of the lexicon available to describe it.

Takeaway

If getting in touch with our subconscious can benefit us, why aren’t we all doing it?

In the Western world, most of us not only fail to seek subconscious help, but we actively inhibit our ability to be open to subconscious messages, mysterious connections, and other phenomena that don’t fit within the strict limitations we keep in our thoughts. We end up with this limited way of thinking because it simplifies our life experience.

However, it is this limited experience that leads to much strife in the world, as many of us think in a simplistic way. For instance, it is simple to believe that everyone should think in the same way or that there is only one right way to behave. We then may become agitated when we meet someone who holds a different view.

I believe the world would be a better place if all of us were in closer touch with our subconscious minds.

item.title: Too Much Information: Therapist Transparency and Oversharing
item.description:
Therapy

Too Much Information: Therapist Transparency and Oversharing

Why it's sometimes better not to know too much about your therapist.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Historically, therapists have shared relatively little about their personal lives with their patients.
  • Therapist abstinence can create rich opportunities for growth and working through.
  • Whether or not to reveal personal information ought to depend on whose needs are being centered.
Source: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash

The first time I ventured through the door of a psychotherapist’s office, I was 22. My therapist was a middle-aged woman with glasses and fine, straight hair. She wore bulky sweaters and sensible shoes. I knew she was married because she wore a wedding ring, but that was all I knew. She said very little, revealing almost nothing about her thoughts as I prattled on, but I experienced her as a steady presence companioning me while I navigated the confusion of young adult angst.

The Blank Screen

Freud taught that the therapist should be a “blank screen” upon which the patient could project whatever she needed. Throughout the profession’s history, most therapists have avoided displaying family photos in their office, refrained from casually sharing personal information, and declined to answer questions straightforwardly about where they were going on vacation. The matter of therapist self-disclosure in therapy is not a simple one, and much ink has been spilled theorizing about when, whether, and why it might make sense to share. However, in general, therapists have been trained to be thoughtful, sparing, and intentional when revealing personal information.

In recent years—with the advent of social media—new norms have taken hold in the business of therapy. On Instagram and other social media sites, therapists now routinely reveal their own histories of substance abuse, trauma, and mental health struggles. They may divulge details about their sexual preferences and political beliefs. They make “relatable” content that features videos of themselves dancing, enjoying a glass of wine, or talking about their life from their car.

In some ways, this trend is refreshing. The injunction against self-disclosure sometimes meant that therapists held themselves too aloof and inaccessible. When a vulnerable patient worked up the courage to ask his therapist a personal question and was met with an evasion or a flat refusal to respond, the result could be hurt and humiliation. However, even if Freud’s blank screen principle could sometimes be misapplied, there is often a benefit to knowing less about one’s therapist, and I can’t help but wonder whether the social media self-disclosure trend doesn’t represent a diminishment of our profession’s technique.

When Less Is More

The reasons for therapist abstinence are complex and multi-faceted, and in this essay, I’ll explore just one: When we know a lot about our therapist, their life can take up too much room in the process. Even intentional sharing can crowd out the patient’s experience. If your therapist has shared on Instagram about their Alcoholics Anonymous meeting, are you going to feel inhibited talking about the great night out you had at the bar with your friends? If you know your therapist also has a history of sexual trauma, are you going to find yourself worried about her as you tell your difficult story? The less you know about your therapist’s personal life, the more space there is for the relationship to be whatever you need it to be.

Early in my career, I had a chance to do an unintentional experiment that showed me quite clearly how important it can be to leave some questions unanswered. As a new therapist, I split my time between two different locations of the same clinic. After working there for a few years, I got engaged and made plans to move to another city. My supervisor at one location instructed me to let my patients know as soon as possible that I would be leaving in a few months, but without telling them why. My supervisor at the other location encouraged me to be forthright and share the reason for my upcoming departure right away.

In the first clinic, my patients expressed anger, disappointment, grief, and even anguish. When they asked me why I was leaving, I invited their theories and imaginings, but I didn’t share my happy news. One patient with whom I had developed a strong rapport spent months working through my leaving. He spent several sessions sobbing, reliving older losses and experiences of abandonment. He spent some sessions raging at me. He finally found the courage to tell me what our connection had meant to him. Our process was painful and intense but took both of us places we likely would not have gone otherwise.

When my departure was just a week or two away, he asked me again. “So, why are you leaving?” This time, I answered. “I’m getting married,” I told him. “Oh!” he said. “I’d love it if that happened to me some day.” His matter-of-fact acceptance of my announcement was hard won at that point, and his ability to imagine himself experiencing a similar happy life event was a tribute to the difficult relational dance we had engaged in over many months.

Whose Needs Are Being Served?

At the second location where I divulged my reason for leaving right away, my patients all congratulated me and expressed their delight at this new development. Once they knew why I was leaving, there was no room for them to be angry at me. They couldn’t express their sense of betrayal, sadness, or resentment. There was no space for them to have a process. Their reactions didn’t change or complexify as the months went on. My departure was simply about me, and not about my patients and their needs and experiences. In many ways, this was easier and more comfortable for me, because I didn't have to deal with my clients' difficult reactions or sit with feelings of guilt. But my needs should not have been primary.

It can sometimes be helpful for a patient to know something personal about their therapist. The question is always whether such revelations are in service to the patient and her process or in service to the desires and wishes of the therapist. It isn’t always a straightforward matter to determine whose needs are being centered, but as clinicians, we need to do our best to parse this. Knowing a lot about your therapist’s personal life may help you feel comfortable reaching out to them when you otherwise might not have had the courage. Knowledge of their struggles can normalize challenges for those who may feel alone with their difficulties. But there are also advantages to knowing less—and opportunities that get lost when we know too much.

item.title: The Catch-22 of Workplace Relationships
item.description:
Career

The Catch-22 of Workplace Relationships

Work friends take work.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Workplace friendships support careers but can also become a hidden source of strain.
  • Workplace cliques can shape who advances and who gets left behind.
  • Women often shoulder the invisible relational labor of maintaining workplace relationships.

By Krystal Duarte, Colleen Tolan, and Lisa Kaplowitz

Workplace relationships are key to a successful company. Healthy work relationships are linked to higher retention, improved mental health, and higher job prospects in leadership. For women especially, workplace relationships and peer networks offer critical support in environments where mentorship and sponsorship remain unequal. Our research from the Rutgers Center for Women in Business (CWIB) confirms this: friendships matter and peer support often acts as an important buffer to burnout and caregiving-work conflict, both of which disproportionately affect women.

Yet, there’s an important aspect of workplace friendships that often goes unacknowledged.

Friendships at work are effortful, and the emotional and cognitive labor required to obtain and sustain healthy work friendships can result in a critical tension for women. For one, women frequently serve as “the social glue” of their teams by performing relationship hygiene, the often invisible work of maintaining social connections (e.g., checking in on colleagues, planning events, welcoming new team members, and resolving interpersonal friction). This work is important as it fosters team cohesion, enhances collaboration, and reduces turnover. Moreover, having friendships at work makes employees 43% more committed and 27% more satisfied with their jobs. Yet, the importance of healthy work relationships for female success is often unrecognized, and therefore overlooked as a critical skill, despite the fact that women who take on relational roles at work report significantly higher stress levels than their male colleagues.

This creates a professional catch-22: the exact friendships that are vital to women’s success can become an added source of strain.

Differences in How Men and Women Form Friendships at Work

Part of the challenge occurs in the formation stage of relationships. Broadly speaking, research shows that men tend to form friendships through shared activities and group accomplishments and are often more comfortable with hierarchy in those relationships. Women, by contrast, tend to prioritize emotional support and equality, values that clash with workplace cultures of competition and scarcity.

When women display ambition or deviate from expectations of warmth and cooperation, they risk backlash and social penalties. Research reflects this cost of ambition: nearly 90% of women worldwide report being penalized or undermined because of their achievements at work. Unsurprisingly, women tend to avoid workplace friendships that feel competitive, viewing competition with peers as less acceptable. This creates a persistent tension between warmth and ambition, often resulting in unhealthy competition, exclusion, and cliques.

When we surveyed 638 working professionals, including 346 women, about the barriers they faced when trying to advance during the mid-career phase, a critical period for promotions and leadership growth, many cited issues directly tied to being on the outside of workplace cliques. For example, we heard responses like, “supervisors (who) already have in mind who they want to promote, like their friends,” and “subjective promotions and raises, with strong cliques that are difficult to overcome.” These responses highlight how relational and organizational dynamics intertwine to shape career trajectories.

Women’s Strategies for Navigating Workplace Relationships

To navigate these dynamics, women sometimes adopt “tend-and-befriend” strategies prioritizing harmony to mitigate stress and maintain belonging.

As a result, women frequently take on the emotional and relational labor required to maintain harmony at work (vital to team culture but often invisible and unrewarded).

This requires emotional labor and strategic impression management, requiring women to balance when and how to assert themselves without violating gendered norms of warmth, modesty, and likability.

It’s also essential to recognize that not all women experience these dynamics the same way. Women of color often bear compounded burdens, not just the expectation to maintain relational cohesion, but also the additional stressors from having to navigate microaggressions, cultural exclusion, and racialized dynamics. One primary example of this is code-switching, where marginalized groups try to adjust their language and self-presentation to fit into the dominant culture in an effort to meet narrow ideals of professionalism. This dual pressure leads to heightened emotional fatigue, making workplace friendships both more complex and more consequential.

These are not simply additive burdens but intersecting ones, shaped by overlapping identities, and as such, require nuanced responses from organizations.

The Advice: Reshape Workplace Culture

1. Recognize the Value of Relationships. According to our research at CWIB, healthy relationships are a key piece to keeping talented women in the workforce. Leaders should recognize their importance and encourage activities that foster healthy relationships like team-building activities and mixed mentoring groups. Specifically, it is important to design intentional collaborative efforts, where differences are valued and employees are rewarded for learning about one another's strengths.

2. Value and Reward Connection. Formally valuing the relational work that sustains teams creates a company culture where healthy workplace relationships can thrive. To do this, discourage cliques, popularity contests, and favoritism as informal pathways to advancement. Instead, companies can encourage employees to build connections rooted in collaboration and mutual support. When organizations both curb exclusive dynamics and reward authentic relational labor, workplace friendships shift from a hidden burden to a supportive tether. Make this work visible and rewarded by incorporating relational contributions into performance reviews, leadership evaluations, and advancement pipelines.

3. Share the Care. Women don’t need to be the default social glue. It isn’t necessary that women be the ones to take on invisible labor or act as emotional caretakers in the workplace. Yet often, non-promotable tasks like organizing birthday celebrations, planning team outings, or tending to morale fall informally to women. While these skills are valuable, it adds to both cognitive labor (the thinking work) and emotional labor (the feeling work); when they overlap, they create the mental load—a constant cycle of anticipating and managing for others. Acknowledging this sort of work as valuable is the first step to redistributing it more equitably. Rotating responsibilities for workplace social upkeep and intentionally distributing this labor more evenly helps to create an equitable environment that doesn’t rely on, and unintentionally perpetuate, gendered expectations that contribute to burnout.

Breaking the Catch-22

The catch-22 of workplace relationships endures because opting out comes at a cost—mentally, emotionally, and financially. But when organizations begin to see relational labor as leadership, not just “extra work,” they create environments where connection and ambition can coexist.

item.title: The Gentle Power of Embracing Our Feelings
item.description:
Relationships

The Gentle Power of Embracing Our Feelings

How turning toward difficult emotions can deepen healing and connection.

Posted July 6, 2026

Key points
  • Avoiding difficult feelings can disconnect us from ourselves, others, and life itself.
  • Healing begins when we meet fear, shame, and sadness with mindful, gentle presence.
  • Turning toward difficult emotions can deepen connection, resilience, and inner peace.
Source: Tiffany Christie Freeman/Pexels

We naturally gravitate toward pleasant experiences and turn away from unpleasant ones. Our aversion to what feels distasteful often leads to dissociation—distancing from feelings that might be uncomfortable or overwhelming. As a result, we may disconnect from ourselves, which can contribute to anxiety, depression, and barriers to the intimacy we desire.

What we casually call our “feelings” are the ways life speaks to us. When we push away feelings, judge ourselves for having them, or try to bypass them, we distance from life—and the rich connections that life offers.

When We Push Away Our Feelings, We Push Away Life

As I describe in The Power of Gentle Presence: Insights for Inner Peace and Deeper Relationships:

“An emotionally intelligent practice—one that fosters deeper connection with ourselves and others—isn’t about ridding ourselves of unpleasant feelings, but embracing them with the subtle power of gentle presence: a way of being with ourselves infused with kindness, warmth, and compassion. And then staying open to where that leads.

Emotional healing doesn’t come from bypassing our feelings or trying to delete inconvenient parts of ourselves. Instead, it emerges when we have the courage to be present with what arises. In doing so, these emotions can soften and shift, revealing a deeper aspect of what we casually call our ‘self.’”

During my 46 years as a psychotherapist, I’ve found that fear, shame, and sadness (including hurt and grief) are often the vulnerable emotions we're most inclined to avoid or minimize. Not only are these primary emotions uncomfortable, but we may judge ourselves for being weak to accommodate them—rather than appreciate ourselves for having the strength to face them. When we try to bypass such emotions, they don’t just disappear—they scurry underground where they may wreak havoc with our lives and relationships.

Eugene Gendlin, the author of Focusing, describes it this way:

“What is true is already so. Owning up to it doesn't make it worse. Not being open about it doesn't make it go away. And because it's true, it is what is there to be interacted with. Anything untrue isn't there to be lived. People can stand what is true, for they are already enduring it.”

Cultivating Mindfulness and Courage

I often tell my psychotherapy clients that there are two essential ingredients needed for healing and growth: mindfulness and courage. Bringing awareness to our feelings is the antidote to dissociation. But here’s the important thing: it is our quality of presence that allows us to face our feelings without dread or trepidation. Bringing a gentle, caring presence to uncomfortable or difficult emotions allows them to soften, settle, shift, or open up.

If a child comes to us upset or crying, we’re unlikely to tell them to suck it up or get over it. Then why have such an attitude toward ourselves when our own inner child is hurting or afraid? By listening openly—perhaps putting our gentle arms around the child—they begin to settle down. Similarly, offering kindness and reassurance to ourselves allows our volatile or uneasy emotions to settle.

Perhaps experiment with placing a gentle hand on your abdomen or chest when you’re hurting, fearful, or upset by some life event. Take a breath. Tap into a gentle courage to be with what’s already there.

Bringing a courageous mindfulness to our experience just as it is often leads to what Gendlin called a felt-shift. The research that led to Focusing found that when clients get out of their heads and drop down into their bodily felt experience—speaking from their inner felt sense (a term coined by Gendlin and now used in many therapeutic approaches)—they made measurable progress in psychotherapy.

Try This

The next time you notice uncomfortable or difficult feelings, notice what happens inside you. Is there an instinctual turning away from them? Do you experience them as a threat? Notice what happens if you can allow yourself to notice what you’re feeling and bring some measure of gentle acceptance toward them. Even if you notice fear or aversion, perhaps you can bring a caring presence to the fear itself.

If much of what I’m describing seems obvious to you, allow me to offer what I often tell my clients: Bringing a gentle presence to our feelings is simple, but not always easy. What we’re up against is our instinctual fight, flight, or freeze response when we face real or imagined dangers.

It’s an ongoing practice to stay present with our ever-changing emotional landscape. But doing so is a pathway toward a deeper inner peace, a richer inner life, and deepening relationships as we find the courage to embrace and share our most tender feelings.
